The team is good. Obviously, every team has a different start in the season but still we know what this team can do. Last year they achieved Europe so it is a really big thing.

We know the players and, yeah, we know how hard these games can be but we are here to try to win and to take all the points.

It is going to be a tough one. Also, the weather, I think. The wind is unbelievable but we are ready. We are here and ready to fight.

We go into every game confident and ready to fight for the three points. We are here to win. We are going for every game [because] we want to win so we will try our best and fight.

Right now, I think his intensity against the ball, his workload against the ball, is on a way better level in comparison to how it was when he arrived and as soon as he adapts, I’m pretty sure his quality will shine through sooner rather than later.

Leeds are always a good side, it was in the Championship and now in the Premier League.

They are doing really well, they are consistent as well. They built momentum early in the season, which is always good, so they are in a different position but anything is possible in football. We think that it is going to be a new opportunity to get better.

Sunderland were warned about “second season syndrome” and shrugged them off in the summer as they looked forward to their first European campaign for more than 50 years.

They had dismissed the gloomy pre-season predictions the previous year and had gone on to enjoy their most successful season in the top flight since the heady days of the Peter Reid era at the start of the century.

So when the “experts” told them it would be much harder this season—that they would no longer have the element of surprise and the squad would be badly stretched by the extra games in the Europa League—it was easy to ignore.

You cannot blame them. It has been a magical couple of years on Wearside where everything has gone in their favour, but reality has hit hard this season.

Sunderland are bottom of the table heading into this home game against Leeds United and have not won in the league since August.

The limp defeat at Bournemouth last weekend brought things to a head, with defender Nordi Mukiele suggesting in a post match interview that his teammates had become arrogant and had forgotten how hard they had to work last season to be successful.

There was a better performance and a decent draw away to Lech Poznan on Thursday night but Regis Le Bris’ side desperately need a win in the league.

Leeds United have been one of the story’s of the season so far and have looked dangerous in every game so far.

The return to fitness of Brian Brobbey is a big boost for Sunderland, but I don’t think any side would like to face Leeds at the moment. The home crowd will be anxious.

Régis Le Bris has made three changes to his Sunderland side.

Brian Brobbey returns to the starting line-up after recovering from a hamstring injury, while Luke O’Nien and Nilson Angulo also come into the side.

Omar Alderete and Timur Tutierov are named among the substitutes, while Kevin Danso begins a one-match suspension following his red card at Bournemouth.

Manager Daniel Farke has made three changes to his starting line-up.

Jaka Bijol replaces Nico Elvedi and starts alongside Tarik Muharemovic and James Justin. Brenden Aaronson and Harry Wilson both start in place of Anton Stach and Noah Okafor, supporting Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the Leeds United attack.

Sunderland: Roefs, Hume, Mukiele, O’Nien, Reinildo, Xhaka, Sadiki, Le Fée, Rigg, Angulo, BrobbeySubs: Ellborg, Methalie, Alderete, Diarra, Ahoka, Talbi, Fofana, Angulo, Tuterov

Leeds United: Trafford, Justin, Bijol, Muharemović, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Wilson, Aaronson, Calvert-LewinSubs: Zetterer, Bard, Longstaff, Stach, Gruev, Cresswell, Nmecha, Okafor, Bahoya

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Sunderland and Leeds United at the Stadium of Light.

The final game of this gameweek sees these two Northern giants lock horns once again in a very intriguing encounter, with Sunderland especially in need of three points.

Following their opening season back in the Premier League last term, Sunderland enjoyed a historic campaign, placing seventh to qualify for European competition for the first time in 53 years. Therefore, their workload for the 2025-26 season has increased, which has caused their domestic form to suffer.

Sunderland currently find themselves bottom of the top-flight table, with just one win and four points from their opening seven league matches. They’ve lost their previous four Premier League games, but a win here could lift them out of the drop zone, depending on other results at Old Trafford and Selhurst Park.

Meanwhile, in the Europa League, it’s a completely different story. Regis Le Bris’ side are unbeaten, earning seven points from the first nine available. They drew 1-1 with Polish outfit Lech Poznan on Thursday evening, and given the relentless juggling act of domestic and European football, they’re already back in today against a very well-drilled team.

Leeds have made a solid start to the season and find themselves eighth in the Premier League, having only lost one match — a narrow 2-1 defeat to Arsenal at the Emirates earlier this month. Last time out, Daniel Farke’s side drew 1-1 with Manchester United at Elland Road, meaning they’re still searching for a first Premier League win since September 14.

Speaking in his preview, Farke said: “To win any point in this league, you always have to be on it. And you always have to be close to be perfect, especially for normal sides - not like the top two. And for that, we are very respectful. So we don’t go into the trap and think we are bigger than we are. We are just the second year back on Premier League level. And we fight for every point.”

#1292. Tragic footballer Jesus de Miguel's devastated club Tenerife vow to financially support his one-year-old daughter until she turns 18 - as fundraiser passes £125,000

Published: 03:12 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 03:12 EDT, 8 November 2026

Tenerife have committed to financially supporting the one-year-old baby daughter of Jesus de Miguel following the 30-year-old's tragic death this week.

De Miguel, 30, lost his life following a horror collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono in the latter stages of a second division game on the Spanish island.

The striker's girlfriend, Maria Fernandez, and their daughter, Carla, witnessed the incident from the stands. A post-mortem found De Miguel died from 'accidental chest trauma'. It is described in the preliminary report as a 'cause consistent with the player's death'.

The footballing world came together in Tenerife on Thursday for the 30-year-old's funeral, with De Miguel's team-mates, Spain national team coach Luis de la Fuente and Real Madrid president Florentino Perez offering support to his devastated family – who said his passing has left an 'impossible void to fill'.

And now Tenerife have confirmed they will support De Miguel's family and Carla following their loss.

Club CEO Antonio Manuel Porro Granados told The Athletic: 'Our plan is to stand by the girl and make sure the entire Tenerife family supports her. We want to be there for her at least until she reaches adulthood.

Tenerife have vowed to support Jesus De Miguel's one-year-old daughter following his death

Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel was struck by Jesus Owono during a second division contest and lost his life

'This is a commitment we have made at the initiative of our majority shareholder, Rayco Garcia, and one that we all fully support. It is a commitment that Tenerife, as a club, is making to the family and to their daughter, Carla.

'We will provide the maximum possible support in every respect, beyond what we are legally obliged to provide. We are also exploring other ways of increasing the financial support, so that, at least in material terms, the circumstances do not affect their lives quite so much — although, of course, it is impossible for them not to have an impact.'

Tenerife's commitment follows the development that a fundraiser for the family has passed £125,000 in donations. Spanish footballers Alvaro Morata and Alex Baena are among those who have pledged to the crowdfunding campaign.

De Miguel's family are also reportedly set to receive around £300,000 in base compensation following his death.

Goalkeeper Owono has shut down his Instagram account and retreated from public view amid the significant backlash he has received – which saw him subjected to chants of 'murderer' by the Tenerife fans as he left the pitch.

On Wednesday, he issued a statement describing his 'enormous pain' following the tragic on-field collision.

Owono said: 'These are being the most difficult days of my life. I am struggling to find the words and find it very difficult to assimilate anything that has happened.

Tenerife say they will financially support the family, while a fundraiser has amassed more than £125,000 in donations

'I feel an enormous pain for the loss of Jesús. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him. I know there will be many issues to address; I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect.

'But right now, honestly, I cannot think of anything else except Jesús and the pain we are experiencing. Rest in peace, Jesús.'

Police investigating De Miguel's death are probing the emergency medical response as well as the possibility rival goalie Jesus Owono's horror tackle could be involuntary manslaughter.

It emerged on Tuesday that homicide squad officers based in the Tenerife capital Santa Cruz had launched a probe as court officials explained any death 'not resulting from natural causes' automatically triggers a judicial investigation.

Legal experts have said they don't expect the ongoing investigation to lead to criminal charges against Andorra FC goalkeeper Owono because the clash occurred during open play, although he is expected to be hit with a lengthy ban.

Como made history with Wednesday’s 9-1 victory away to RC Lens, their sixth straight win in all competition.

#1290. Fine-tuning brain stimulation to fight Parkinson’s disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Liam Drew is a freelance science journalist based near London.

Stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (orange) can lead to changes in multiple nerve tracts.Credit: Nanditha Rajamani

Sixteen years ago, Simon Little was a junior neurologist thinking of devoting his time to international health work. But then he attended a lecture by Peter Brown.

Brown, a neuroscientist at the University of Oxford, UK, described his studies of people with Parkinson’s disease who had had electrodes implanted in their brains. The electrodes were intended to treat symptoms of this neurodegenerative disease by targeting electrical pulses to structures deep inside the brain. But to start with, Brown used them to record the oscillating waves of neuronal electricity that these brain structures emitted.

The recordings showed that as a person’s symptoms ebbed and flowed — their movements slowing then normalizing, their tremors flaring and subsiding — the oscillations changed1. “I was completely fascinated,” Little says. “The music of the brain was encoding something really powerful about people’s symptoms.”

After the lecture, Little asked Brown if he could do a PhD with him. Little laughs as he recalls how Brown tried to warn him off, saying that the field was a complete backwater and that Little would be pursuing this work at his own professional risk.

Undeterred, Little joined Brown’s laboratory, and the risk paid off. Little, now at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), and Brown took the signal most strongly related to the intensity of Parkinson’s symptoms — an oscillation in what’s termed the beta band, occurring 12–30 times per second — and used it as the trigger for deep brain stimulation (DBS).

Typically, DBS zaps the brain constantly. But by activating the device only when beta activity crested, Little and Brown could provide stimulation when a person most needed it. In an initial trial, numerical ratings of volunteers’ mobility were about 30% better than they were with constant stimulation2. “We found that less was more,” Little says.

Last year, the first ‘closed loop’ or adaptive DBS (aDBS) system for Parkinson’s, which operates similarly to the set-up that Little and Brown used in their early experiments, was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and earned a CE mark to be sold in the European Union. The technology — made by Medtronic in Minneapolis, Minnesota — uses the same electrodes to record beta-band activity and stimulate the brain.

Although this system is clinically effective, researchers think that it provides only a fraction of what smart implanted neurotechnologies could one day offer people with Parkinson’s. “This is a breakthrough,” says Wolf-Julian Neumann, a neuroscientist at Charité University Medicine in Berlin. “But it’s a super-tiny step towards the vision that we are pursuing.”

Neumann, Little and others say that emerging techniques and hardware now being tested in small clinical trials will lead to devices that decode, on the basis of neural activity, what someone with Parkinson’s is doing — say, sleeping, walking or speaking — and the exact symptoms they are experiencing. Then, with this real-time information, devices will deliver different forms of electrical stimulation to alleviate users’ symptoms and aid their movements3. “It’s a totally different way of conceptualizing the treatment of brain disorders,” says Neumann.

Parkinson’s disease is characterized by degeneration of the brain’s substantia nigra, a cluster of neurons that produces the neurotransmitter dopamine. This dopamine regulates the brain networks that coordinate voluntary movements. Without it, that system malfunctions.

“In Parkinson’s disease, you’ve got an unwanted brain arrhythmia,” says Helen Bronte-Stewart, a neuroscientist at Stanford University in California. The extent to which neurons synchronize their firing at beta-band frequencies is abnormally high, producing a disruptive signal, she says. “It’s jamming the brain’s ability to coordinate movement.”

This leads to the hallmark symptoms of Parkinson’s: slowed movements, rigidity and tremors. The disease can also cause postural changes, speech difficulties and non-motor symptoms, such as depression or anxiety. In its later stages, cognitive decline is common. The standard treatment is to boost a person’s dopamine levels by dosing them with the drug levodopa. But levodopa can cause side effects, such as uncontrolled movements, and people can experience periods in which the drug’s effectiveness blinks on and off.

Since its clinical approval in 1997, DBS has emerged as a popular alternative for people whose Parkinson’s isn’t well controlled by drugs. Far and away the most common type of brain implant in use today, DBS has done much to normalize the process of undergoing neurosurgery to have a therapeutic device fitted. In its original form, the DBS electrodes — connected by wires that run down the recipient’s neck to a small power pack implanted in the chest — deliver a constant, high-frequency train of electrical pulses. Their target is either the subthalamic nucleus or the globus pallidus, two brain regions that are components of the movement network modulated by dopamine.

Simon Little (right) follows his patient Deb Zeyen as she demonstrates motor improvements.Credit: Yalonda M. James/Polaris/eyevine

Andreas Horn, a neuroscientist at the University of Cologne in Germany, says that ‘stimulation’ is a misnomer in DBS. The high-frequency zapping, he says, “is more about disrupting or overriding some circuitry that’s become dysfunctional”.

The change from continuous DBS to aDBS demanded that Medtronic incorporate the necessary technology into a compact medical device. Little says that in his first experiments, volunteers were wired up to racks of computers, filters and stimulators. Medtronic miniaturized that hardware so that it all fitted into the small implanted power pack.

Bronte-Stewart led the trial that secured the device’s approval4. This showed that aDBS was safe and that it controlled recipients’ symptoms effectively. The trial — somewhat controversially, Bronte-Stewart acknowledges — didn’t directly compare aDBS with conventional, continuous DBS. But just sending people on aDBS home and trusting they’d be safe was a groundbreaking step, she says.

Since 2020, Medtronic has been supplying a system capable of running either continuous or aDBS, and roughly 25,000 recipients could potentially switch to aDBS now. However, scientists are already taking note of the limitations of this system — and of using beta-band oscillations as a trigger.

One issue is that current aDBS systems take weeks of inpatient programming, with neurologists observing the effects of different sets of manually selected stimulation parameters5. “For this to scale, you can’t have every Parkinson’s patient needing three weeks of a neurologist monitoring them and optimizing this,” says Doris Wang, a neurosurgeon at UCSF.

Another issue is that beta oscillations provide only a crude indication of overall symptoms. “Beta power is essentially a biomarker of global worsening of symptoms of Parkinson’s disease,” says Neumann. Although this information is no doubt useful — not least, says Neumann, for effectively up- and downregulating DBS as levodopa’s effects change — beta-band oscillations don’t discern exactly what someone is experiencing. “Tremor actually reduces beta,” he says. As a result, “the beta-based adaptive DBS algorithm can confuse tremor for a good symptom state.”

What’s more, in current systems that use the same electrodes to stimulate the brain and record activity, artefacts from the stimulation compromise the quality of recorded signals6. Plus, these systems are recording from sites in the brain that are selected because they are best places to stimulate, and not necessarily the most informative to record from.

To address these issues and offer much finer control of the disease’s various manifestations, researchers are seeking to develop next-generation aDBS systems. On the input side, they are harnessing advances in brain–computer interfaces, including fresh technologies for recording and decoding brain activity. These, the researchers say, will be able to decipher exactly what users are doing and what symptoms are occurring.

On the output side, clinical studies are showing that it’s possible to halt symptoms of Parkinson’s by targeting separate neural pathways. For instance, Horn’s group has found that, by targeting adjacent but distinct nerve-fibre tracts (using conventional continuous stimulation), they can selectively help with tremor, rigidity, slow movement, or postural and gait-related problems7. “This is not so much about when to stimulate,” Horn says, “but rather about where and what to simulate.”

To map which nerve-fibre tracts passed close to the DBS electrodes, Horn’s team took brain scans of people who had had Medtronic devices implanted in the subthalamic nucleus. The scans showed tracts originating from different parts of the brain, such as the motor cortex or cerebellum, running near to the four contact sites on each electrode.

The researchers then stimulated various combinations of contact sites to steer currents to different chosen tracts. To their surprise, targeting specific fibre tracts ameliorated symptoms individually.

Horn and colleagues then developed an algorithm that, given a set of symptoms, will choose stimulation sites that should provide the most benefit. “If a patient has a lot of tremor, we tell the algorithm, ‘find me the stimulation volume that will maximally engage the tremor tract and not so much the other tracts’,” says Nanditha Rajamani, a neuroscientist at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts, who collaborated with Horn on this project.

In a small, five-person trial, the algorithm’s suggested settings produced a bigger improvement in the symptoms of four participants than did the stimulation their neurologists had previously set up for them7. The fifth person’s symptoms neither improved nor worsened.

Looking ahead, Horn says that because the manifestations of Parkinson’s shift constantly, the ability to target each symptom type could enable adaptive devices that suppress only the symptoms a person is currently dealing with. But that will require the device to ‘know’ what those symptoms are, meaning that researchers must identify the neural correlates of each symptom type.

To do so, they are recording brain activity while volunteers use wearable devices, such as accelerometers, to precisely track arm and leg movements. Increasingly, recordings are acquired not just from DBS electrodes deep in the brain, but also from a separate set of electrodes placed on the brain surface. These cortical electrodes pick up the signals that arise in the motor cortex to initiate and control movements. “There is a lot more information in the cerebral cortex,” Wang says.

Neumann’s group, for example, has used machine learning to link hundreds of features captured in such neural recordings to both symptoms and drug side effects. The features the researchers used correlated with symptoms better than beta activity did. And importantly, the model worked in people whose data had not been used to develop it.

Neumann thinks that this approach might even allow researchers to identify neural signals that precede symptoms. If so, future systems might not just react to symptoms as they occur, but could also pre-emptively stimulate the brain to prevent tremors and other typical manifestations of Parkinson’s from occurring at all. “When you and I intend to move, there’s a huge spike of dopamine release,” he notes. A well-timed burst of electrical stimulation could functionally substitute for this in people with Parkinson’s and thereby ease upcoming movements.

Neuroscientist Helen Bronte-Stewart assesses someone with Parkinson’s disease.Credit: Yalonda M. James/Polaris/eyevine

Neumann also thinks that if a smart DBS system can decode what a person is doing, or trying to do, this could help to select the stimulation activity that best serves that person. For instance, he says, the high-intensity stimulation that suppresses tremor can make it difficult to speak, so if brain signals indicate that a person is attempting to talk, then the tremor-suppressing stimulation might be turned down, or even off.

Likewise, Bronte-Stewart, Little and Wang are searching for neural correlates of movements and symptoms, with a view to controlling stimulation8. Little and Bronte-Stewart are also keen to treat symptoms of Parkinson’s that are not related to movement by finding appropriate signals and target structures to combat mood symptoms and cognitive difficulties, respectively9.

In June, Wang published a small trial that began to put the pieces together. It used movement-related brain signals to address a hugely problematic aspect of Parkinson’s: gait freezing, in which people who are walking suddenly become unable to move and so fall10.

After identifying cortical and subcortical signals that indicated the motions of walking, Wang’s group used them to trigger brief stimulation on the relevant side of the brain — the right side to affect the movement of the left leg, and vice versa. People who received this intervention fell less frequently than those who did not. “It’s the first demonstration that such rapid, movement-specific aDBS or closed-loop DBS is possible,” Wang says. Trial participants said that movement felt smoother and more fluid when using the system, and that it was easier for them to get up and walk.

It’s safe to say that Brown was wrong when he told Little that attempting to relate brain signals to disease symptoms was a dead end. But over the years, what it takes to bridge the gulf between exploratory research and a clinical product has become more apparent. “Our role as researchers is to show what’s possible,” Little says. Only then can the different questions regarding what can be scaled up into a viable clinical intervention begin to be addressed.

Already, there are questions about next-generation DBS that did not apply to the first adaptive systems. For instance, Little notes that if extra cortical recording electrodes are needed, surgeons will need to learn a new implantation procedure.

He is also wary of emerging systems being heavily dependent on artificial intelligence — either to decode brain activity or to get systems up and running without weeks of manual programming. Concerns swirl about embedding uninterpretable AI technology in medical devices, especially when people’s welfare and behaviour depend on it.

Little questions what would happen if someone using an AI-powered DBS system experienced a major mishap, such as freezing completely or crashing their car, because the algorithm changed its stimulation patterns. “Who bears responsibility for that?” Little says. This is an evolving space for both developers and regulators, who must find a sweet spot with which all parties are comfortable, he says.

The transformation of an idea into a clinical product is a balancing act between what’s possible and what’s plausible, reliable and safe. As Parkinson’s researchers aim to again lead the way in new forms of neurotechnology, they will need to navigate the known and unknown challenges that arise. As Bronte-Stewart says, today’s advances “are coming out of really good labs in academic centres doing a lot of computational work. How is that going to filter down into something that can be embedded in a system in your chest?”

#1289. Michael Carrick reveals club bosses have not told him if he will still have a job next week, with Man United languishing in relegation zone ahead of Aston Villa clash

Published: 17:30 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 04:50 EDT, 8 November 2026

Michael Carrick has not been given any guarantees over his future beyond Sunday's game against Aston Villa at Old Trafford as Manchester United dropped into the relegation zone.

United bosses handed Carrick more time to turn the club's season around following the 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth a fortnight ago amid speculation he could be replaced by Eddie Howe or Julian Nagelsmann.

In the two games since then, Carrick's side have lost at Chelsea and staged a rousing comeback over Roma in the Champions League to secure a first win in 10 games.

United slipped into the bottom three after Nottingham Forest beat Manchester City on Saturday, and could be in last place by the time they kick off against Villa depending on the outcome of other games involving Sunderland and Crystal Palace on Sunday.

The situation could leave Carrick's position under threat during the two-week international break. Asked if he has been told outright that he will be in charge next week, the United boss replied: 'No. Just carry on as absolute normal.

'Whatever is going to happen is going to happen. I'm really looking forward to the next game, playing at home on the back of the other night.

Michael Carrick revealed that club chiefs have not told him if he'll be in charge next week

Sir Jim Ratcliffe (left), Omar Berrada (centre) and Jason Wilcox (right) have not informed their manager about their plans for the international break

'The supporters are hopefully looking forward to coming energised and feeling good about what they might see, and we've got to repay that.'

Carrick is preparing for a normal international break, and doesn't have any plans to spend more time with his family after a turbulent period at Old Trafford.

'Not really different to normal. Genuinely not,' he added. 'I think international breaks are always a time to re-energise and freshen up. Some of the players that go away to internationals get freshened up in a different environment, but I don't really need it. I'm fine as I am.

'We'll certainly train next week and maybe have the weekend off. We'll see how that develops, who's left behind, who's with us and what they need.'

Carrick insisted that he and Bruno Fernandes have put any issues behind them after the United captain criticised his tactics in the Champions League defeat to Como last month.

After he led United's fightback against Roma in midweek by converting a twice taken penalty, Fernandes confirmed that Carrick's decision to drop him for the Bournemouth game was due to a loss of form, and disputed that the two men had a clear-the-air meeting over his comments.

But Carrick said: 'There are always conversations, bits going on; acknowledging certain things of when things are going well, what we need to improve on as a group.

'Sometimes it's individually, sometimes it's group. We always have discussions. What's actually said in that discussion, I'll keep that to myself.

'But I think it's pretty clear we've moved in a good direction, and Bruno's commitment is undoubted for me (in terms) of what he brings to this team and this club.

'He showed that again this week by his actions, the way he's played and how he dealt with even retaking the penalty and the frame of mind he was in for that. I think that tells you everything. Bruno's as good as ever.'

#1288. Vanoli: ‘Fiorentina need experience and balance’ against rivals Juventus

Paolo Vanoli explains some of his unexpected Fiorentina picks against Juventus, insisting they need ‘experience’ to control this very important fixture.

It kicks off at the Stadio Artemio Franchi at 19.45 GMT (20.45 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from today’s five Serie A games on the Liveblog.

This is never a regular fixture due to the bitter history between the two clubs, which is why the Viola are so pleased with their recent results against their rivals.

They are unbeaten against Juventus since April 2024, managing two wins and as many stalemates.

“I experienced this game as a player and a coach, I always tried to explain to the players what it means to wear this jersey, especially in a fixture like this,” Vanoli told DAZN Italia.

“We need to represent it proudly in every game, above all one like this where we can write history.”

Pedro Goncalves is a surprising pick, while Christ Inao Oulai is another unexpected starter instead of ex-Juventus midfielder Niccolò Fagioli.

“When I talk about balance, it also means mental strength. Goncalves is accustomed to this type of pressure, so I hope his experience can help him to handle the role. However, the most important thing the whole team needs is courage.

“A player cannot be 100 per cent in every game, sometimes he needs a breather to recapture his sharpness. Oulai deserved an opportunity, he had very different characteristics, but I would say neither Oulai nor Fagioli are traditional playmakers,” explained Vanoli.

“We are a team built to keep the ball and I like to defend with the ball at our feet, whereas sometimes we get a little over-excited and try to attack at all times.”

Fiorentina have had another chaotic campaign, as Fabio Grosso was sacked on September 6 after just four competitive games, bringing Paolo Vanoli back to the Stadio Franchi.

This initially brought a boost, then two points from five rounds until Monday’s 4-2 success away to troubled Sassuolo.

Published: 04:55 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 05:11 EDT, 8 November 2026

Euro-winning Lionesses goalkeeper Mary Earps has named her son Xander after becoming a mother for the first time, having revealed this week that her partner has given birth to a baby boy.

Earps, 33, was a hero of England's Euro 2022 victory at Wembley and starred at the World Cup in 2023, saving a penalty in the final. She won BBC Sports Personality of the Year but later lost her England place to rival Hannah Hampton and retired in acrimonious circumstances.

She moved to France with Paris Saint-Germain but returned to England earlier this year - and has now welcomed her first child with her partner, Kitty Forrest.

'Welcome to the world, Xander,' she posted on Instagram, with a photograph of her newborn's hand.

In a video released on Friday, Earps said: 'I've been keeping a little secret from you all. And I don't think I can talk my way out of this one. So, I think I'm going to have to show you.

'I can't quite believe I'm writing this, but yesterday Kitty and I welcomed our beautiful baby boy into the world!

'We're absolutely over the moon and still trying to take it all in. It's been such an emotional journey getting to this point, and we couldn't be more excited to start this next chapter of our lives as a family of three.'

Mary Earps has revealed the name of her baby boy following his secret birth: Xander

Earps and her partner Kitty (second right) revealed news of welcoming a baby boy (YouTube/Mary Earps)

Earps says she will not be able to take maternity leave due to the rigors of the football season. Her team, London City Lionesses, are eight games into the new Women's Super League season and sit third behind Chelsea and Manchester City.

'In any other job, you would just be like, "Okay, bye. Taking maternity leave, whatever. Um, and you just do what you need to do." But that doesn't really work in football, because you've got games and then, if you take the day off, then you got to think about what that looks like and how that works into sort of your training schedule and the fixture calendar.

'So, it's a little bit more complicated. You can't just take annual leave whenever you want without consequence. You know, it's going to be interesting to see what the next days and weeks bring.'

Earps first revealed that she was in a same-sex relationship in September of last year but largely kept partner Kitty out of the spotlight.

Earps is pictured kissing the trophy after England won Euro 2022 at Wembley Stadium

Earps won BBC Sports Personality of the Year in 2023 following her Euro heroics

'The people closest to me have always known, and I feel ready and happy to share that with everyone else now.'

Earps retired from England duty in May last year after the release of her autobiography dragged up a storm with Hampton, the Chelsea goalkeeper who overtook her from understudy to become England No 1.

#1286. Hapless and hopeless Man Utd bring curtain down on out-of-depth Carrick

Hapless, hopeless and utterly humiliated. And that has to be that for Michael Carrick. It is surely inconceivable that he will continue any longer as Manchester United’s head coach. A proud club on its knees and a favoured son on his way out.

The former midfielder will carry the can. As managers always do. Even if the fault lines run so deep at United that it feels like they are almost irreparable. Owners – the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – executives, players. A collective failing of monumental proportions. Although, again, it will be the manager who goes. Carrick knows it and it looked like it at the end. He knows the score, especially after this score.

More than four years ago Ralf Rangnick, the then interim manager, declared that United needed “open heart surgery”. Now there is barely a pulse.

An announcement must be imminent, with United turning to someone else in the fight against Premier League relegation. A joke? No, this abject performance against Bournemouth leaves United in 16th place, just a point above the bottom three, so the priority for the new man will be clear. Save them from the drop. They are 14 points off the top already, but forget that. It is irrelevant given their plight.

That is how far United have, once again, fallen. Fans in the Stretford End unfurled their “Standards” banner, bearing the faces of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and Bryan Robson.

It was first revealed in December 2021 in Carrick’s final match as interim following Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s sacking. This should be his final game again, under different, more traumatic, circumstances.

If it is, he is going out having made a stand. He dropped Bruno Fernandes for his outspoken comments, aimed directly at Carrick and his tactics, following the dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat away to Como on Wednesday.

At 2-0 down here it was telling that Carrick turned to Matheus Cunha when he substituted Youri Tielemans, who had been so terribly slow and ineffective, at half-time. Carrick did not bring on Fernandes. And he did not turn to the captain after, as he made four substitutions, including bringing on 19-year-old Shea Lacey. That said it all.

The television cameras catching Omar Berrada, the United chief executive, shaking his head in the stands as Carrick’s team gave away goals also told its own story. They have two wins from 12 in all competitions and none in eight. They have only beaten newly promoted Ipswich Town, in August, and Azerbaijan minnows Sabah this season. United were so careless it looked like they could not care less.

There was no guarantee, after Como, that Carrick would remain in charge after this game. So, losing and losing so embarrassingly – it was three, it should have been five – has to have obvious consequences. However cherished Carrick is. However much the fans excuse him. Yes, he has not been helped enough, but he has also not been good enough.

Finishing third and qualifying for the Champions League last season has proved to be the kind of bounce a new manager can achieve, after the pressure was relieved by the sacking of Ruben Amorim, rather than something more sustainable. There was always the fear that Carrick, despite his playing pedigree, might be out of his depth in this job. And so it is proving to be. Especially as he has been hung out to dry. Carrick certainly appeared resigned to his fate.

But what is he coaching? What is he trying to do with United? How does he want his team to play? Yes, there are limitations, but they are badly set up, tactically poor, and struggle to build attacks. The players are not responding, but it does not mean Carrick is blameless.

Bournemouth were not just collectively and individually better – and despite how good they are, that is some indictment of United – but better organised. They knew what they were doing, believed in it and relished it as they collected a fourth victory, and a fourth clean sheet in a row, after a slow start under Marco Rose, the new head coach. It was no shock.

The nature of the goals spoke volumes. For the first, a free-kick was needlessly conceded by Ayden Heaven, who endured a particularly difficult game, as he lunged in recklessly, forcing Evanilson to jump out of the way or risk injury.

Justin Kluivert whipped the ball in beyond the far post and it was met by Rayan, who volleyed in low and precise. The Brazilian was unmarked. Carrick protested – at what? – and the Bournemouth supporters sang “you’re getting sacked in the morning”.

It was the same as Carrick walked down the tunnel, thumping his chest as his name was sung. Then it turned. The vitriol, frustration and anger dripped down on the players, washing them away.

This felt like a new nadir. And the need for yet another new start away to Chelsea on Saturday.

Former Tottenham defender speaking to the BBC:

Manchester United’s players were just standing there today. I did not see in their body language that they are prepared to do everything for the manager, the club or the fans to change their situation.

It’s an easy thing to say they are lacking leaders but it’s true. They just don’t have big characters. It is not something technical but if you are in a tunnel and you saw the likes of [former Man Utd defenders] Nemanja Vidic or Rio Ferdinand their body language told the opposition that they were going to have a tough afternoon.

Carrick admits he does not know if he will remain in place.

The club have a week off now, with the next match a trip to Stamford Bridge against a tasty Chelsea side, albeit one who lost to Spurs last night.

He says: “It’s a tough situation. What is next? I don’t know. I’ll always do what’s best for this football club. I don’t change that now. I love what I do. I love the responsibility. But we’ll have to wait and see.”

Carrick gives a non-answer over his choice to leave Fernandes on the bench.

He says: “There’s always times when you’re trying to make decisions that are to change the course of play and made a difference but those are the decisions we made today.”

Carrick then denies that his acknowledgement of the crowd was to say goodbye, adding: “It wasn’t a farewell from me. I’m mixed emotions, I’m feeling it for my players, they’re going through a tough spell.

“Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment. Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way.”

Carrick also tells Sky: “It’s really difficult to have a day like this at this football club and feel the emotion and dynamics of what it was like today.

“Not for me personally but for Manchester United. It was really mixed. I feel responsibility with the position I’m in. I’ve been at the club a long time. It hurts a lot going through this.”

Carrick potentially acknowledges that his time is up, telling Sky: “It was a strange, mixed of emotions at the end of the game. It wasn’t a nice way to end the game.

“It was a tough day for the players. We went into the game having been rocked. You can feel that. They’re really hurting and disappointed in there. It’s not a nice feeling. You have to accept it, we’re in that situation.”

Today’s United captain Harry Maguire tells Sky Sports: “It wasn’t good enough. Disappointed to give a goal away so early - another set play - and conceding first in the Premier League it makes it difficult.

“A mistake for the second makes it hard for ourselves. We didn’t perform well enough as individuals or as a team and we didn’t deserve anything from the game.

“It’s not clicking at the moment. Results are not good enough and performances in the last week not good enough. Still early in the season.

“Got to find something, question yourself, look in the mirror - that’s the most important thing - think what you can do more and what more you can contribute to the team and if we do that we’ll get somewhere.”

United players have said this for some time now. Each season they look in the mirror, and each season the supporters get the same.

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Manchester United’s crucial Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Michael Carrick has taken the decision to drop the United captain to the bench in the wake of his public criticism on Wednesday following the shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics and has now been taken out of the starting XI.

The move had looked likely with Carrick refusing to rule out stripping Fernandes of the captaincy when quizzed on the matter on Friday.

Carrick had responded to Fernandes questioning the set up and approach by suggesting tactics can go out of the window when players are unprepared to run.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

United enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

With just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

In stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

Bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). #1285. Premier League legend David Silva, 40, makes emphatic return to football with man-of-the-match performance - three and a half years after retiring

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 08:23 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 10:15 EDT, 8 November 2026

David Silva made his mark in his first game since coming out of retirement after scoring on debut in a man-of-the-match display for Hong Kong outfit Sha Tin on Saturday.

Last month, the Manchester City icon revealed he was lacing his football boots in a professional sense again for the first time since 2023.

The 40-year-old started for Sha Tin and broke the deadlock against HK Rangers from the penalty spot in the 56th minute.

Silva stepped up and coolly passed the ball into the bottom left-hand corner - sending Hong Kong Rangers goalkeeper Ka-Yu Yip the wrong way.

The playmaker's goal sparked mass celebrations from his team-mates and the fans in the stands - with many taking their phones out of their pockets to record the moment.

However, Silva's debut didn't go as smoothly as planned as the visitors equalised in the 65th minute through Ibrahim Yakubu Nassam.

Some Spanish guy just scored a penalty for Sha Tin#DavidSilva #hkpl #hkfootball pic.twitter.com/JCbiYZEKE0

David Silva scored for Hong Kong outfit Sha Tin with this penalty in their 1-1 draw on Saturday

The 40-year-old celebrates with his team-mates after scoring against Hong Kong Rangers

Silva was named man-of-the-match, in what his first competitve match in over three years

With 11 minutes remaining, Silva was then booked before he was substituted in the 84th minute with his side down to 10 men following Maxwell Ansah's 81st-minute red card for a second bookable offence.

Despite failing to take all three points, Silva did collect the man-of-the-match award after the full-time whistle.

Sha Tin currently sit 10th in the Hong Kong Premier League with five points from their opening seven matches. They sit one point and place above bottom-placed Eastern AA, who occupy the sole relegation spot, and 14 points adrift of table-toppers North District.

Silva called it a day on his playing career back in 2023 when he tore his anterior cruciate ligament while playing for Real Sociedad.

He is most famed for spending ten years at Manchester City between 2010 and 2020, where he won 11 major honours; four Premier League titles, two FA Cups and five League Cups. Much of that time period, though, is now under scrutiny.

He also has a statue outside the Etihad Stadium, and won the 2010 World Cup with Spain, as well as Euro 2008 and Euro 2012.

Upon joining Sha Tin, ex-Valencia midfielder Silva said in an Instagram video: 'I'm so excited to go to Hong Kong and enjoy the local culture, the food in Sha Tin and, of course, football in Hong Kong.'

Silva will hope to lead his side to victory when they take on Southern District in the Hong Kong League Cup Losers play-offs on Saturday.

#1284. Spalletti: ‘Juventus need to put faith in players, you say we must win Scudetto’

Luciano Spalletti explains his Juventus choices against Fiorentina with an all-new trident attack, and sarcastically hits back at critics. ‘You all say we need to win the Scudetto.’

It kicks off at the Stadio Artemio Franchi at 19.45 GMT (20.45 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from today’s five Serie A games on the Liveblog.

The Bianconeri have a very poor recent record against their bitter rivals, not managing a victory since the 1-0 in April 2024, followed by two draws and as many defeats.

Weston McKennie and Zeki Celik are back in the squad, while Nick Woltemade came down with flu symptoms and is in the starting XI anyway as part of a new trident with Jeremie Boga and Randal Kolo Muani.

That means sending Kerim Alajbegovic to the bench this evening.

“We played two days ago, another three days before that, so we need to rest these players at some point,” Spalletti told DAZN Italia.

“Boga scored a great goal off the bench, he went t sit back down, so every now and then we have to put our faith in these players.”

Juventus had been plunged into crisis by the 3-0 home defeat to Lazio and 2-2 Rennes draw, but recovered with back-to-back wins over Napoli and AZ Alkmaar.

“It is a game where the volume will be turned up, in the crowd, on the field, it somehow becomes a bigger city when this game is one. So we must avoid getting manipulated or dragged into the frenetic nature of this fixture, we’ve got to keep our heads, and hopefully raise the quality level of our performance.

“You all say we need to win the Scudetto, so we’ve got to play with the quality that this squad does possess,” replied Spalletti with sarcasm to the Juventus critics.

“Being frenetic robs you of the right choice, it stops you seeing things clearly, so this can be a turning point for us.”

Juventus are still missing Kenan Yildiz, Andrea Cambiaso, Nico Gonzalez, Manuel Locatelli, Khephren Thuram and Kamil Grabara, with Jeff Ekhator only just returning from a long spell out.

“Ekhator is a physically strong centre-forward who can run into space, he has the strength to take a position against defenders and can hold up the ball. He is young, so he feels the pressure, as he probably did with these two injuries, he needs a little time, but we are happy to have him available as an alternative with different characteristics.”

Joana Gonçalves-Sá is in the Laboratory of Instrumentation and Experimental Particle Physics (LIP), 1649-003 Lisbon, Portugal, and the Complexity Science Hub, Vienna, Austria.

Ana Maria Jaramillo is in the Complexity Science Hub, 1030 Vienna, Austria, and Graz Technical University, Graz, Austria.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are designed to isolate cause and effect. They have become important instruments for evaluating interventions in medicine, economics and public health. Their strength comes from assigning ‘treatments’ independently of the characteristics of the participants. However, people live in communities, and interventions delivered to individuals can have consequences far beyond the outcome that researchers set out to measure. Writing in Nature, Papamichalis et al.1 highlight this phenomenon.

#1282. Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year wait for Ballon d’Or winner

“Wow, wow, wow,” Harry Kane said as he took to the stage at the London Palladium after winning the 2026 Ballon d’Or. Wow indeed. “I am speechless,” Kane added before launching into a heartfelt speech, the wobble in his voice showing just how much this meant to him.

In truth it would have been a travesty had the 33-year-old England captain – and Bayern Munich striker – not won with his family, friends and coaches all watching from the stalls at this famous old theatre. “All those years of sacrifice,” he said of his parents, Pat and Kim, his voice faltering more than ever at that moment. It was from the heart. And faltering again as he spoke about his wife and “best friend” Katie Goodland. “This is a trophy we all celebrate,” he said, talking to his children back in Bavaria. “I bring a few others [trophies] home but this one is a special one.”

Kane’s speech was as outstanding as his football. “Lastly for me it is the journey,” he said. “Learn through resilience, determination and self-belief. My journey was not easy and I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration.”

So much for the “one-season wonder”. So much for the doubters who poured scorn on him. So much for those who believed he would never make it after loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City. With varying degrees of success.

Kate Scott, the presenter, perfectly detected the emotion and said: “You held it together. You got through it.” It showed how much it meant to Kane, who simply and quietly replied: “Yes”.

What a winner. What a player. What a role model. The award given in the city where he has scored most of his goals. But he would not have been in the running for this accolade had he not been brave enough to quit Tottenham Hotspur after 19 years and move to Germany.

Kane was the favourite. But, despite its prestige, the Ballon d’Or process is an odd one. One journalist from each of the top-100-ranked Fifa countries is given a vote, with the organisers, France Football, laying out the criteria: individual performance, collective performance and fair play. In that order. They often go for the biggest name. Not the best.

Kane’s numbers are incredible. They speak for themselves. Those numbers show he deserved to win the prize: 65 games for club and country and 73 goals. Plus eight assists (for the judging period – August 3, 2025 to July 19, 2026). That is 61 goals for Bayern and 12 for England. That is a goal less than every 72 minutes. That is beyond elite. That is world class and legendary.

Bayern Munich and England's Ballon d'Or winner doing what he does best 🎯 https://t.co/yWNburqkpg

For his club, that is 19 goals more than any other player in the top five European leagues. And the most since Cristiano Ronaldo scored 61 for Real Madrid in 2014-15. Kane won last season’s Golden Shoe by nine goals from Erling Haaland. He reached his century of Bundesliga goals last month in just 98 games, destroying Dieter Müller’s record set 49 years ago – he took 129 matches.

Kane became one of only two players in history (the other is Ronaldo) to score 20-plus goals across World Cups and European Championships and was the only one to score in two major club cup finals, including a hat-trick. Neither Kylian Mbappé nor Lamine Yamal, his closest rivals, scored in any finals.

Both gave interviews declaring why they should win the Ballon d’Or. Kane? “I don’t like talking about myself,” he said. “The 73 goals speak for themselves.” They do.

Those are the facts, but there is also the football and, yes, the conduct. Kane has scored some superb goals during that period, not least for England. Take his two goals against the Democratic Republic of Congo at the World Cup that saved his team and Thomas Tuchel from an embarrassing early exit.

The Prince of Wales, who has been FA president since 2006, congratulated Kane on “a fantastic achievement”.

“A brilliant captain, a remarkable player and someone who has given football fans across the world so many unforgettable moments,” Prince William wrote on Instagram.

Kane, the first English player since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the award, is also the ultimate team player – so fulfilling that “collective performance” criteria – and a captain who leads by example on and off the pitch. Fair play? He was last booked in January and was cautioned just three times in 68 games and not at all in any of his 13 appearances this season.

And he works hard, so very hard. Kane was in the top 10 for total distance covered at the World Cup, despite playing a game fewer than most of the others on the list. And he is often seen winning as many defensive headers in his own penalty area as attacking ones in the opposition’s.

That work extends to off the pitch, to try to maximise his ability, to do everything to be the best version of himself and to be the best. Which he has now been recognised as. And it stems from his winning mentality. Some scoffed when Kane walked into England’s press conference before the 2018 World Cup and said he could be top-scorer – but he proved them wrong.

They probably also scoffed at the notion that he would one day be declared the best player in the world and win the Ballon d’Or. But he has done all that. It confirms England’s all-time cap holder (for now jointly with Peter Shilton) and goalscorer as one of the greats. And we are privileged to witness that greatness. Wow, what a night.

By Christian FalkGermany do not have a single player among the 30 in the running to win the Ballon d’Or in London on Monday night – but Bayern Munich do have England captain Harry Kane.

For the 35-time German champions, the award is perhaps even more important than it is for the peerless striker himself. The Bayern hierarchy are planning to travel to the Palladium Theatre en masse to support Kane.

Kane is not only Bayern’s top striker, he is their international figurehead and, internally, their poster-boy professional. Club patron and honorary president Uli Hoeness described the England captain as the best signing in the club’s history. Hoeness even went so far as to say he loves Kane, and he is not alone in this.

There's only one Harry Kane. https://t.co/NfZEFmjaUN

Hoeness is one of many in the club’s leadership who have been endlessly promoting Kane to help the 33-year-old fulfil his lifelong dream of winning the trophy. Bayern officials have been campaigning on his behalf for weeks.

First up was manager Vincent Kompany, who remains in hospital for tests after collapsing at Bayern’s training ground on Friday. Kompany said: “If he can now crown his career or his season with the Ballon d’Or, that would be fitting given the way he plays for the team.”

The plaudits kept coming. Whether it was sporting director Max Eberl (“He has more than earned the Ballon d’Or. Anyone who loves football loves characters like Harry Kane”), chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen (“One thing is clear – anyone talking about this year’s greatest individual honours cannot overlook Harry Kane”) or president Herbert Hainer (“Harry Kane embodies the idea that sporting greatness is incomplete without greatness of character. He would be a worthy World Footballer of the Year”), everyone at the club is fighting for Kane.

The official Ballon d’Or website has announced Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal as winners of the main prize in an embarrassing blunder for the organisation.

Three separate articles were published before quickly being taken down.

The headline on Kane’s article read: ‘Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d’Or: Here are his best and most meaningful strikes from a 61-goal season’.

The 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony takes place at the London Palladium as England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane aims to become the first Englishman in more than 20 years to win the award. Michael Owen was the last Englishman to win the award back in 2001.

The choice of London as the host city pays tribute to the award’s inaugural winner, England’s Stanley Matthews, who won it in 1956. This also marks the first time the ceremony will be organised outside France. Kane, who scored over 70 goals for club and country in the relevant year, is among the favourites for this year’s award alongside the likes of Barcelona and Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid and France’s Kylian Mbappe.

Kane won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich whereas Yamal won both La Liga and the World Cup. Yamal won the Kopa Trophy at last year’s ceremony as the best men’s young player.

Last year’s winners were Spain and Barcelona midfielder Aitana Bonmati and France and Barcelona forward Ousmane Dembele. Dembele is aiming to become just the 11th man to win the top prize at least twice, although it would appear to be very unlikely that the Frenchman will be winning the award this evening.

Selected international journalists cast their votes based on the performances of players throughout the season. The panel consists of one representative per country from the top 100 nations in the Fifa men’s world ranking and the top 50 in the women’s world ranking. Each voter ranks their top 10 candidates, with points distributed on a descending scale. They vote based on three factors: individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.

In total, 13 trophies will be presented across the men’s and women’s game, including the two man Ballon d’Or awards, the best young players and best teams. The awards take into account achievements from August 3, 2025, to July 19, 2026 (August 16 for the women).

#1281. From last place to the playoffs: How the Philadelphia Union pulled off MLS's most stunning turnaround

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

CHESTER, Pa. -- At the end of the World Cup, the Philadelphia Union were at the bottom of the Eastern Conference and all of Major League Soccer with only seven points, moving on from Supporters' Shield-winning head coach Bradley Carnell and turning to 36-year-old Ryan Richter to save the season. Given Richter's path as someone who oversaw the Union's MLS Next Pro side before becoming an assistant under Jim Curtin with the first team, it seemed like a moment where the Union would be in the process of preparing for next season and seeing what they did next.

But with the return of a familiar face in Kai Wagner, a meeting at Two Persons Coffee in South Philadelphia between captain Alejandro Bedoya and Richter, and one of the most impressive runs that we've seen of youth talent in league history, the Union were able to clinch a place in the MLS Cup playoffs, and they did it in impressive fashion, too, by playing Nashville SC to a scoreless draw away from home without 17-year-old phenom Cavan Sullivan being available for the match. It caps off a turnaround that has seen the Union pick up 40 points since the World Cup, winning 12 matches, drawing four, and only losing one. Those 40 points outpace the second-best team in the time range, which is Nashville SC, by five.

Sullivan has been one of the spark plugs of this improvement with seven goals and 11 assists, with most of that coming after the World Cup break, but with 38 of the Union's 59 league goals absent for that game as Bruno Damiani and Milan Iloski missed out on the match, it truly showed the mentality that the squad has.

Plenty preach about "next-man-up" mentality, but matches like this one show why no one should want to face the Union in the playoffs. If the season ended today, they'd face Inter Miami in a three-game series, which would be sure to bring fireworks after the scuffle that their last meeting created, but there's still more work to do with two games remaining, as the Union could slide down to the eight-versus-nine play-in game if they lose their final two games of the regular season.

Under Carnell, the Union were a traditional high-press team that tried to force their opponents into mistakes. While it worked with only MLS games to play, adding in the Concacaf Champions Cup saw the team unable to keep up that intensity, especially without Wagner at left back and with Neil Pierre on loan in Denmark instead of being with the squad. While Richter did benefit from both of these players being in the mix, he has also dialed things back to more of a zonal press, allowing the midfield to have time to rest in between plays so that they can keep the same intensity at minute 90 as they have entering the game.

Pierre and Nathan Harriel on the back line have assisted greatly with that, being mobile centerbacks in their own right. Richter knows the impact of having a 6-foot-7 defender like Pierre, who is also comfortable when being on an island, and it's clear how he helps the attack function.

"We can be super aggressive because Neil is comfortable in one-on-one situations. If it's a direct ball, he wins; he eats all of these. If it's open space that he has to defend, physically, he can deal with that, and he's also a good defender," Richter said. "The way he puts out so many fires allows us to be aggressive higher up the field, because we know when they play the ball long that we have someone who cleans this up almost every time."

Putting that in front of three-time MLS Goalkeeper of the Year Andre Blake, it's easy to see why the Union's defense has improved from the first half of the season, but the attack is where major strides have been made.

You'd have to be living under a rock to have not heard the name Cavan Sullivan by now, and for good reason, as the 17-year-old has been taking MLS by storm and helping push the Union attack forward with his creativity. Since the World Cup break, Sullivan is second only to Evander in assists with nine and has pitched in goals alongside that. He may not be the biggest or fastest player on the pitch, but the quick bursts that he has into space have been tormenting defenses.

Alongside Pierre and Frankie Westfield, he was able to earn his first national team cap under Mauricio Pochettino and also didn't look out of place there either, but when speaking to him and people around the team, the shift in mentality is clear. Sullivan asked to do extra training during the World Cup break instead of taking the time off, and has come back a more complete player. Already set to join Manchester City when he turns 18 next year, the path for future development is clear (assuming City are in the Premier League), but this is one of the best American soccer prospects ever developed. Being able to play alongside his older brother Quinn also helps with this transition, but Cavan has grown into a player of his own, and while this season has been a coming-out party for him in many ways, the playoffs are going to be a moment that can thrust him into the stratosphere as he looks to lead his hometown club to the first MLS Cup title in their history.

Which American has the most goals in Major League Soccer? Usually, the answer to that question is Brian White, but this season, it also resides in Philadelphia in Milan Iloski, a longtime journeyman, he has found a home in Philadelphia and has scored 19 goals with seven assists, which is third in the league. After moving Tai Baribo to D.C. United, there were valid questions of where the Union's goals would come from, and Iloski has delivered and shown that there isn't a finish that he doesn't have in his locker, and he's not overperforming, either, with an xG of 18.77.

Alongside him, Bruno Damiani has stepped up with 12 goals, and the Uruguayan could be key to any serious playoff run that the team has. If teams crowd Sullivan and Iloski, other people on the team need to be able to make them pay, and Damiani is chief among them. The hope was that new signing Ezekiel Alladoh would be able to take on that mantle, but with one goal and one assist in 26 appearances, he may find minutes hard to come by in the playoffs unless there's an injury. While it's unlikely that they'd upset the likes of Nashville and Miami to win the MLS Cup, the mantra of "Why not us" has always carried Philadelphia and looking at these numbers, you can't say that they don't have a chance. Given that, it is also only a matter of time until the interim tag is removed from Richter's coaching title, but that's an offseason issue to deal with; right now, there are more soccer games to win.

#1279. Inside the insane trophy room of Chelsea legend Branislav Ivanovic: Framed pictures of his 42 goals, a ring from Didier Drogba... and an LED football pitch

Published: 04:50 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 12:08 EDT, 8 November 2026

Legendary Chelsea defender Branislav Ivanovic's insane private trophy room has gone viral after a fan posted a tour of the museum online.

The now 42-year-old made 377 appearances for the Blues during a nine-year stint at the club from 2008 to 2017.

He enjoyed a hugely successful time with the west London side, winning ten trophies and becoming one of the club's most decorated defenders.

As well as winning three Premier League titles he landed three FA Cups,  the League Cup, the Community Shield and the Europa League. He also has a Champions League winners' medal with the Blues, though the Serb did miss out on playing in the 2012 final after famously being told by Geoff Shreeves live on Sky Sports that he was suspended following their win over Barcelona in the semi-final.

Branislav Ivanovic won 10 trophies with Chelsea across nine years with the Blues

The Chelsea legend has built a private trophy room in his hometown of Sremska Mitrovica to rival any other

In a video posted to Instagram a fan from Ivanovic's hometown Sremska Mitrovica explained he was allowed access to the private showroom and documented the breadth of trophies, personal honours and shirts he has collected throughout his illustrious career.

Many of the souvenirs are from his time in Russia with Lokomotiv Moscow and Zenit St Petersburg, as well as those he got at Chelsea.

The private museum holds over hundreds of shirts alone and has an entire wall adorned with shirts just given to him and signed by someone he either played with or played against including the likes of Zlatan Ibrahimovic, Neymar and Javier Zanetti.

Most Chelsea fans will remember Ivanovic's most crucial goals such as his winners in the Champions League round of 16 against Napoli and the 2013 Europa League final against Benfica.

And the Serbian appears to have made an effort to immortalise every single one of his club goals by framing and displaying a photo of all 42 from throughout his career.

Amongst other quirky designs, the room has a set of football leg stools for guests to sit on at the bar

Mourinho gets a mention having won the Premier League, Fa Cup and League cup with the Serbian in the 2014-15 season

There is also a replica of every trophy he has won in his career as well and a specialty ring he received as a gift from Didier Drogba after Chelsea's 2012 Champions League triumph.

Ivanovic didn't forget to add some style to the room by installing an LED football pitch to light the room and putting swanky football leg chairs at a fully stocked bar.

He even has a slide solely dedicated to displaying quotes from his former manager Jose Mourinho including the Special One's description of Ivanovic as 'The Perfect One'.

Since leaving Chelsea in 2017 the Serb moved back to Zenit St Petersburg before ending his career back in England with West Brom in 2021.

#1277. Winning is the only thing that matters to Rangers midfielder Dan Neil as Ibrox club continue to gain momentum in title challenge

Published: 13:52 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 14:02 EDT, 8 November 2026

Rangers midfielder Dan Neil admits he couldn’t care less about how his side go about picking up points as long as the wins keep coming.

The stand-in captain netted the crucial second in Saturday’s hard-fought victory over St Mirren in Paisley after Ryan Naderi had given the visitors a first-half lead from the penalty spot.

It was a result which extended Rangers’ unbeaten run to 12 in all competitions as they continue to build momentum following an unconvincing start to the campaign, and Neil insists that’s the only thing that matters at this stage.

He said: ‘I think every good team just finds a way to win.

‘Obviously, we’d like to win by four or five goals every single week but unfortunately that’s just not football. I do think it’s an area that we can improve on.

‘There’s been too many games this year where maybe we don’t get that second goal and it’s a bit nervy. Teams get a little bit of confidence off that and the momentum shifts.

Dan Neil savours the moment after putting the seal on Rangers' win with the second goal

‘I think it’s definitely something that we can improve on, putting teams to bed when we do go 1-0 up and go 1-0 up early doors when we’re creating chances.

‘But at the same time, finding a way to win is the most important way and whether that’s 1-0 or 5-0, at the end of the day it’s three points.’

While Rangers weren’t quite at their best in Paisley, they did more than enough to halt their poor recent run away from home.

Back-to-back 2-2 draws at Dundee and Hearts last month saw valuable points dropped in what is shaping up to be a tight title race, and Neil was delighted to get back to winning ways ahead of the international break.

‘The last two away results and performances really haven’t been us,’ said the former Sunderland man. ‘It was important that we didn’t have another one of them going into the break and have it lingering over us. Everyone played their part in making it a comfortable result.

‘Coming away from home in any league is tough, but especially this league. It’s important that the mentality of the group is right, which it is, and I think you’ve seen that on Saturday night.

‘It was important to put that hoodoo of those two results behind us and make sure that we win the game. I think there was some good football played for the majority of the game and we also dug in when we had to. That’s credit to every single player in that dressing room.’

#1276. Fabregas: ‘Inter deserved the victory, the strongest team in Europe in transition’

Cesc Fabregas admitted that Inter were the better side after Como fell to a 2-0 defeat in San Siro in Serie A on Sunday evening, explaining that the Nerazzurri have more experience in big matches and that they are ‘the strongest in Europe’ in transition.

Strikes from Pio Esposito and Marcus Thuram within the first 20 minutes gave Inter a two-goal lead against Fabregas’s side, which they were able to hold onto right the way through until the full-time whistle.

You can see how the action unfolded on the Football Italia Liveblog.

Fabregas did not need reminding that Inter were the better of the two sides on the pitch on Sunday. He was, in fact, complimentary of the way that Inter played and the experience they have available in their squad.

“We didn’t start the game well, we made a few mistakes and we weren’t confident,” Fabregas told DAZN while assessing his own side’s performance.

“We have to congratulate Inter, who played much better than us. We’re on a different journey than what we’re used to, playing every three games. We have to thank the boys for what they have given us so far.

“Inter deserved the victory, we have to shake their hands and move on. The demands are always rising and we have to continue like that. I’m not looking for any excuses, this is what football is like and a coach has to adapt. My responsibility is to look for solutions.

“We only had two central players, so I tried to help by bringing Smolcic in. The way we lost hurts, with those balls that we gave away too cheaply. That makes you lose confidence because Inter are very strong in transition, the strongest in Europe.”

Fabregas went on to explain that Inter “are one of the best teams around on counter attacks and from set-pieces. They made 13 fouls and did those well because they didn’t get any booking. In these games, just breaking up the rhythm can impact the game. These sorts of details show the experience they have and we’re lacking that.”

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.
