#1168. How the brain protects itself from Parkinson’s disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Sarah DeWeerdt is a science journalist in Seattle, Washington.

The pianist’s hands are poised over the keys, his right hand trembles slightly. A drummer and bass player start up and, after a beat, the pianist joins in, both hands fluently producing the luscious, staccato rhythms of jazz.

The hands in this video from 2019 belong to Dutch musician René van Helsdingen, who had recently been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. He uses strategies that reduce stress and emotion to help quiet the tremors that affect his right side and enable him to continue playing the music he loves, he explains in the video. “It’s my improvised solution.”

Improvisation is an apt metaphor for the ways in which many people with Parkinson’s learn to cope with the tremor, stiffness and movement difficulties that are characteristic of the neurodegenerative disease. Some use an external source of rhythm, such as a metronome, to overcome the tendency to ‘freeze up’ when walking or adopt a sideways crab-like gait. “I’m very inspired” by people’s creativity, says Rick Helmich, a neurologist at Radboud University in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, who has worked with van Helsdingen.

Other improvisations take place in the brain, beyond a person’s awareness, to preserve function in the face of Parkinson’s pathology. If scientists can understand them better and harness them more effectively, they might be able to slow the progression of Parkinson’s disease, delay its onset and even prevent it entirely, say researchers, such as Helmich.

The motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease are caused by a loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra — part of a set of structures nestled deep in the brain known as the basal ganglia. But these symptoms do not emerge until at least 30% of those neurons are lost, and sometimes as many as 70%. Two people with a similar degree of neurodegeneration might have very different symptom severity. And some people’s condition worsens quickly, whereas others remain stable for years. Such observations have led most researchers and clinicians to agree that brain-based mechanisms of resilience must be important.

But for a long time, this area received little research attention because scientists focused instead on unravelling the pathology of the disease and on developing an effective treatment, called levodopa, that remedied the underlying dopamine loss. The awareness that the brain has ways of making up for the neurodegeneration in Parkinson’s hasn’t led to clinical advances, says Thilo van Eimeren, a specialist in brain imaging at the University of Cologne in Germany.

This area is now garnering more interest. It is a focus of a three-year, European Union-funded project launched in 2025, known as TRACE-PD, to track the mechanisms of disease progression and functional compensation in early stages of disease1.

The first task for the team from across Europe was to define its terms. That effort is more than mere semantics, says David Pedrosa, a neurologist at Marburg University in Germany and co-coordinator of the project. More clarity in the vocabulary that researchers use to talk about protective mechanisms will enable them to probe the underlying biology with greater precision, and design better targeted clinical trials to investigate how to bolster these processes, he explains.

The TRACE-PD consortium has defined resilience as an umbrella term that encompasses multiple protective mechanisms. One, called reserve, refers to neuronal resources built up across the lifespan that mitigate the effects of the disease. Another, called compensation, involves changes to neurons and brain networks that stabilize function in response to the disease.

The idea behind reserve makes intuitive sense: when a neurodegenerative process takes hold, individuals who have greater neural resources in a particular domain will take longer to decline to a point at which their impairment becomes obvious. Cognitive reserve has long been a focus of Alzheimer’s disease research. And over the past few years, studies of Parkinson’s have examined the idea of motor reserve.

Most such studies have defined individuals with high motor reserve as those with milder motor symptoms than their degree of dopamine-neuron loss would predict. A 2020 study by researchers in South Korea showed that people with newly diagnosed Parkinson’s and high motor reserve have greater connectivity between areas of the brain involved in movement, planning and control2. Greater connectivity in this network is also linked to a lower need for levodopa treatment.

“Individuals with higher motor reserve levels also show greater grey matter volume in motor-associated areas,” says Merle Hönig, a neuropsychologist at the University of Cologne. She and van Eimeren contributed to a study3 that also found that the gap in disease trajectory between individuals with high motor reserve and low motor reserve takes more than seven years to close, suggesting that assessing motor reserve early could help to determine prognosis.

But could motor reserve be the basis for interventions to alter the course of Parkinson’s? The same study showed an association between higher motor reserve and higher levels of physical activity in one cohort of people with the disease — a suggestive but circumstantial link. The team now has unpublished data that strengthen the case for a causal relationship by showing that people with higher lifetime levels of physical activity also have higher motor reserve. Exercise is known to slow progression during the early phases of Parkinson’s, but there is much about this connection that is poorly understood, says Patrick Santens, a neurologist at Ghent University in Belgium. “Nobody really knows what is the best,” he says. What type of exercise is beneficial, at what intensity and for which individuals?

Another question is the relationship between the different types of reserve. “We don’t know whether promoting, for example, cognitive reserve also helps to preserve motor reserve,” or vice versa, Hönig says. Research in this area might, therefore, have implications for multiple neurodegenerative diseases.

Research involving compensation goes back to at least the early 1990s. But over the past few years, Helmich says, the concept has been refined. Whereas greater activity in a brain area or network was once seen as evidence of compensation, scientists are now looking for a link between stronger hyperactivity and greater symptom reduction, for example.

This approach has enabled researchers to zero in on the neural substrate of compensation. Helmich and his team have shown that the main brain areas involved are the parietal cortex and the premotor cortex. The less affected parts of the basal ganglia also contribute4.

Another group have investigated brain activity in people with dopamine-neuron loss on both sides of the brain, but symptoms on only one side of the body. The researchers identified several compensatory mechanisms in the brain hemisphere that controls the unaffected side of the body, including increased plasticity in motor networks5.

Helmich and his team have also shown6 that, over the course of two years, “the speed of progression relates to the collapse of compensatory mechanisms”, he says. The researchers have unpublished data from a separate cohort showing that people who have mutations in the gene encoding the enzyme glucocerebrosidase, long known to increase the risk of Parkinson’s, have reduced potential for compensation. Such studies place the loss of compensation at the centre of disease progression.

Researchers are now beginning to investigate how to intervene to stimulate compensatory mechanisms. Helmich and his team identified an ‘anti tremor network’ that comes online when a tremor reduces in intensity and consists of areas of the cortex involved in attention and in interpreting bodily sensations7. He is testing whether an intervention involving mindfulness training and meditation can help people to activate this network and control the tremor.

Stimulating compensatory mechanisms might also involve non-invasive brain stimulation — Helmich plans to launch a study later this year using transcranial ultrasound to activate the less affected parts of the basal ganglia to find out. Meanwhile, Pedrosa is investigating how to use advancing knowledge of compensation to improve deep-brain stimulation, a treatment in which electrodes are implanted in the brain to send electrical signals to areas involved in motor control.

Further research will be needed to help refine and guide these approaches, says Josefine Waldthaler, a neuroimaging specialist at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden. “We know where to look” for compensation in the cerebral cortex, Waldthaler says, but not the particular patterns of brain activity that define it, and therefore what brain frequency interventions need to stimulate.

Magnetoencephalography, an imaging method that is Waldthaler’s specialty, could fill in some of those details. And that’s where TRACE-PD comes in. The effort brings together researchers who use different approaches to investigate various aspects of resilience. Rather than collect new data, the idea is to share existing data sets and analytical methods. This will help the consortium to tease apart the mechanisms of compensation and reserve, validate definitions and refine applications, Pedrosa says. What the researchers find could have broader relevance as well. “The cool thing about the idea of compensation and reserve is that it’s not a Parkinson’s specific idea,” says Pedrosa. He contends that the group’s insights might shed light on other neurodegenerative conditions, such as Alzheimer’s disease, as well as on strategies for healthy ageing.

And although TRACE-PD focuses on early Parkinson’s, the processes it looks at might still be harnessed later in the disease. In May, van Helsdingen performed with his trio in Italy. In a video of the concert, his symptoms seem to have worsened since 2019. He rocks rhythmically back and forth as he plays, and at one point crosses his left wrist over his right to execute a particularly tricky sequence of notes on the upper keys with his less-affected left hand. But the result is syncopated, at times cheerful, music that makes it clear he’s still improvising.

#1166. Marco Rose's Bournemouth should not have the depth to win this many games domestically and abroad but at Ipswich they showed they can do it the hard way, writes JAMES SHARPE

Published: 11:20 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 12:48 EDT, 8 November 2026

Juggling domestic duties with European adventures should not be as manageable as this for teams like Bournemouth.

Clubs of their size should be creaking under the weight of the extra fixtures. All those games, all that travelling. They have played nine games in a month.

Far bigger outfits have toiled spinning those plates. Remember when Ange Postecoglou stopped bothering about the Premier League entirely just to focus on the Europa League.

And yet here are those brilliant Cherries, three days after a win in Prague in that same competition, making it eight on the bounce with a victory at Ipswich thanks to Evanilson's opener, following goalkeeper Christian Walton's early howler, and an own goal from Leif Davis.

Bournemouth haven't done that since 2013 when they were getting out of League One.

Now, they are seventh in the Premier League, second in the Europa League.

Leif Davies reacts after scoring an own goal to make it 2-0 to Bournemouth

And they're in the League Cup quarter-finals – all while having the squad depth to name Alex Scott and Junior Kroupi on the bench.

Marco Rose's side showed they can also do it the hard way, too, after Jack Clarke's second-half penalty for Ipswich, given for a soft foul on Abdoul Ouattara, provided a far more tense final 15 minutes than anticipated inside a feverish Portman Road where Julio Enciso also twice went close from late free-kicks.

'One goal changed the momentum of the game and that's why I'm much more pleased about the last 20 minutes because we suffered but we did it together,' said Rose.

First James Trafford, now Walton. Bournemouth's win over Leeds last weekend also hinged on a goalkeeping howler, when Trafford's simple pass out from the back was intercepted.

This time Ipswich stalwart Walton took a back pass from Dara O'Shea and decided the best course of action was to try to dummy and turn Evanilson. He failed, of course.

Evanilson rolled the ball into an empty net. That intense Bournemouth press really can do some crazy things to you.

IPSWICH (4-2-3-1): Walton 4; Ouattara 5, Diop 6, O'Shea 6, Davis 5; Florentino 7 (Akpom 85), Palacios 6; Maeda 6 (Fatawu 65, 7), Enciso 7; Philogene 6 (Clarke 54, 7); Emersonn 5 (Flemming 54, 6)

BOURNEMOUTH (4-2-3-1): Petrovic 6; Smith 6 (Diakite 79), Hill 7, Silva 7; Truffert 7; Adams 7, Christie 6 (Cook 67, 5); Rayan 6 (Adli 86), Kluivert 6 (Kroupi 68, 6), Tavernier 7; EVANILSON 8 (Rodriguez 85)

After scoring the opener in Bournemouth's win last weekend, manager Marco Rose told Evanilson that he was becoming a 'real No9'.

That's six goals now in his last seven games but it's his all-round play that's so impressive.

He dropped in and played a beautiful curling through ball into the channel to set Justin Kluivert free down the right.

He collected the loose ball for the second goal.

He made a fine run to latch on to a free-kick over the defence to stab the ball over to James Hill at the back post, who headed over from close range, which would have put him level with Declan Rice as the leading assister in the league too.

'He's so hard-working,' added Rose. 'He does everything out of possession.

'He starts the press, he plays in between the lines, he gives us deep runs.

'But the most important thing is scoring and he understood that he also needs to arrive close to goal if he wants to score.'

If the Tractor Boys are to make their stay in the Premier League a longer one than last time, they cannot afford to keep giving early leads. The mountain is steep enough.

Evanilson's opener was the sixth time Ipswich have conceded inside the first 15 minutes of a league game this season. They are yet to score one that early.

A howler from Ipswich keeper Christian Walton gifted Evanilson the opener

James Hill celebrates Bournemouth's win which lifts them to seventh

It is what will make this defeat especially frustrating for Gary O'Neil against his former club. 'Gary, what's the score?' chimed the travelling fans.

#1165. Germany's China calculation shifts as import pressures eclipse export benefits

Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.

Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's  unfair trade practices.

In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate.

Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market if unfair practices continue.

Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means."

China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction."

Before the COVID pandemic, the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent.

Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026.

Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking, precision engineering and chemicals industries.

German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025.

Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of layoffs and possible factory closures.

In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports.

"After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.

Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments."

Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt:

"We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August.

According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026.

While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home.

The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, aims to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies.

Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally."

Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.

Bloomberg last week cited unnamed German officials as saying that a new EU kill-switch could be a "second-strike weapon" if Beijing blocked those exports. Brussels is also considering unilateral limits on how many hybrid cars China can export to the EU, according to the same Bloomberg report.

Perhaps to avoid such an open confrontation, the EU and China reached a "shared understanding" last week at the EU-China trade talks in Beijing that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the European Union by more than half, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, who headed the European delegation.

Reports say the agreement would cap such Chinese imports at 350,000 vehicles annually, with the limit increasing by 6% each year over four years.

Overall, new hybrid-electric cars in the EU reached nearly 37% of all new cars registered from January to August, according to ACEA data.

MERICS, meanwhile, calculated that the EU is a more critical export market for China than the US. In the first half of the year, Chinese exports to the EU were $254 billion (€354 billion), versus $172 billion to the US.

This could give EU negotiators a firmer hand as they seek to avoid a trade war while protecting Europe from China's latest export glut.

"The EU has more leverage than it sometimes thinks," MERICS' Mischer told DW.

#1164. Emery endures heaviest European defeat as Villa manager to old foes Barcelona

While there can be little doubt about Unai Emery’s status as an elite manager in the modern game, matches at the Nou Camp continue to be the stuff of nightmares.

His record at Barcelona now reads 15 defeats from 16 matches and this was another difficult evening with Aston Villa unable to banish the demons for the man who has transformed their club.

It was Emery’s 55th birthday and with the Prince of Wales and Prince George both in attendance, Villa fans were hopeful of another memorable European night. But from the moment midfielder João Gomes handed Barcelona their opening goal, it was always going to be an uphill struggle.

Emery has suffered many uncomfortable occasions at this grand old stadium, none more so than the notorious “La Remontada” of 2017 when he last competed here in the Champions League with Paris St-Germain.

This latest visit would become his heaviest defeat in Europe as Villa manager. With three wins from the opening four matches, they still have a fine chance of progressing to the knockout stage. Yet, aside from the mistakes, there will be a sense that Villa could have capitalised more against a team in the midst of a defensive injury crisis. They did have a number of chances in the first half but were left to rue their lack of ruthlessness.

At the heart of Barcelona’s victory was Lamine Yamal, their outstanding jewel from the academy. The 19-year-old became the highest-scoring teenager in Champions League history, eclipsing the record of 13 he previously shared with Kylian Mbappé, with the opening goal.

Yamal was orchestrating everything from the pace of the match to the volume of the supporters, at one point imploring them to raise the noise in the first half with both arms aloft.

There was also another impressive performance from England international Anthony Gordon and Raphinha, who dedicated his two goals to the memory of Jesus de Miguel, the Tenerife forward, who died on Tuesday.

With that tragedy fresh in the minds and the Nou Camp under construction, it was a peculiar atmosphere at times.

The defeat marked the end of Villa’s 100 per cent record in the competition, with a tough test away at Galatasaray up next before they host PSG in December. They remain high up in the table and have often displayed a propensity to bounce back quickly from defeats.

Emery said: “We are in a process and this was a very good test against a team like Barcelona. We are not at the level we want to achieve but there are a lot of experiences for us to take. Overall, we are competing fantastically in the Champions League and there is still work to do.

“Over the process we’ve had here, we have made mistakes but then overcame them. We accept this defeat but take a lot of information from it.”

Nine years have passed since Emery’s last visit in this competition and time has not proved a great healer.

Then in charge of PSG, Emery witnessed his team surrender a 4-0 first-leg lead to lose 6-5 on aggregate. Any matches where he is involved at the Nou Camp will revive memories of that remarkable comeback. He must have feared a repeat of more pain when Yamal, making his 37th Champions League appearance, rewarded Barcelona’s early pressure.

Villa’s defending needed to be as close to perfect as possible, but they were exposed after a poor error of judgment from Gomes. Under pressure from Barcelona’s attackers, Gomes panicked and played a blind pass into the path of Yamal, who bent his left-footed shot into the corner.

That mistake could have threatened to damage confidence but Villa did respond. Matty Cash’s half-volley from inside the penalty area was only a few inches wide, while Johan Manzambi side-footed wide of the goal after a quick break down the right from Nicolas Jackson.

With Andreas Christensen, Eric García, Xavi Espart and Jules Koundé all absent here, Barcelona’s defence did appear vulnerable. Jackson was targeting the flanks and having his more dangerous moments challenging their high line. Emery paced his technical area, imploring his players to remain focused.

Yet Barcelona’s forward three were always a threat and they increased their lead eight minutes into the second half. Raphinha was given too much room to turn in the penalty area and his shot took a heavy deflection off the heel of Pau Torres to find the bottom corner. Emery was furious, appearing to raise his fist in the air at another poor goal conceded.

#1157. Liverpool played like a team fighting for their manager, but Pierre Sage looks like a dead man walking, writes LEWIS STEELE - as Reds clinch morale-boosting win at sorry Crystal Palace

Published: 11:14 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 13:00 EDT, 8 November 2026

By this time of the season, spirited performances mean little if you don't have the results to go with it.

Pierre Sage, who was sacked at Lyon two years ago, knows as much as anyone that this is a results-based business.

And he simply has not had enough results. Despite having Liverpool on the ropes at times here, Crystal Palace failed to land a knockout blow and that could be that for their under-fire manager, who looked like a dead man walking when he trudged off the pitch at full-time with a face like thunder.

Former Lens over-achiever Sage now seems set for a stuffing six weeks before Christmas and though he may curse at the small margins that denied his team a chance of a heavyweight and potential job-saving scalp here, the boss knows two wins in 10 league games is not good enough.

Liverpool, meanwhile, had the width of the crossbar and a throwback performance from goalkeeper Alisson to thank. In contrast to Sage, Andoni Iraola's side showed grit and determination to win when far from their best.

Alexis Mac Allister, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak all scored as the Reds put a tough week behind them that saw them lose back-to-back games for the first time in the Iraola era, which prompted a chorus of the old terrace classic 'Poetry in Motion'.

Florian Wirtz scored a rare Liverpool as they won 3-1 at Crystal Palace in the Premier League

Wirtz scored Liverpool's second on 54 minutes as they ran out as 3-1 winners at Selhurst Park

Things are looking ominous for under-pressure Palace manager Pierre Sage after another loss

This performance was hardly William Wordsworth levels of poetry and Liverpool were far from on song during large swathes of this match but when it really mattered, the attackers demonstrated just why the club spent so much money on them.

CRYSTAL PALACE (3-4-2-1): Henderson 5; Lerma 6, Richards 6, Disasi 5; Mingueza 6 (Khalali 87), Wharton 5, Timber 6 (Timber 60, 6), Mitchell 6; Kamada 6, Pino 7 (McNeil 87); Larsen 5 (Nketiah 72, 7)

Subs not used: Benitez, Canvot, Chilwell, Doucoure, Hughes

LIVERPOOL (4-2-3-1): Alisson 9; Araujo 7 (Gomez 90), Jacquet 6, Van Dijk 6, Kerkez 6; Szoboszlai 7 (Nyoni 69, 7), Mac Allister 8; Gakpo 6 (Ngumoha 76) Wirtz 8, Barcola 7 (Munoz 69, 7); Isak 7 (Koumas 90)

Subs not used: Mamardashvili, Endo, McConnell, Tsimikas

Booked: Araujo, Barcola, Munoz, Mac Allister

Scorers: Mac Allister 40, Wirtz 54, Isak 89

Mac Allister resumed his bemusing role of the team's best aerial threat despite being their smallest player, Wirtz got a goal and assist, while Isak made it eight for the season to continue his prolific streak.

Bradley Barcola, meanwhile, proved what an asset he is despite a wasteful first half.

Those attackers were worthy of praise but no one deserved plaudits more so than goalkeeper, Alisson, who was player of the match in an illustration of Palace's first-half supremacy.

'I'm very pleased with Alisson's performance,' said Iraola. 'He has commanded the box very well and in games here a lot of things are normally happening in the boxes. He has shown the level he has for us. Overall we are getting good results away from home at difficult stadiums.'

The Brazilian is in the last year of his contract but put in his best performance for 18 months, dating back to a 1-0 win at Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League knockouts. He will not go on international duty and instead rest up after an injury-hit few years.

He denied Adam Wharton with a glancing header, thwarted Daichi Kamada with a fierce shot and then tipped round Quenten Timber's effort from distance. Palace also rattled the bar through Yeremy Pino in a first half that really should have ended up differently.

Jorgen Strand Larsen also had the ball in the net but was offside.

As it was, though, Liverpool were the team to take their chance when it came after a period of dilly-dallying and playing the wrong ball, guilty again of indecisiveness similar to the flaws shown against Arsenal last weekend and in the 3-2 defeat at Fenerbahce in midweek.

Liverpool led on 40 minutes when Alexis Mac Allister (centre left) scored from close range

The Argentine celebrates after breaking the deadlock for the Reds in the Premier League clash

Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage is facing the sack after his side dropped to the bottom of the Premier League.

Palace have won just two of their ten league matches this season, with Sunday's 3-1 defeat to Liverpool leaving them at the foot of the league for the first time in nearly nine years.

Sage is expected to lose his job during the international break, with Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank leading the race to replace the French coach.

However, Sage believes his side have been unlucky with results this season and has requested the hierarchy remain patient.

The 47-year-old, who left RC Lens for Palace in the summer to succeed Oliver Glasner, also admitted the Palace squad needs strengthening - perhaps to absolve himself of some blame.

'You can create the links between these two things,' Sage replied when asked whether being bottom of the league heading into the international break could see him sacked.

'But a lot of times I've said we deserved better and it was the case again on Sunday.

'My job is not the most important thing, as I always said from the beginning. The most important thing is to find an efficient solution for the team and for the club.

'I know how important it is for the club to stay in the Premier League. The club just have to believe in that, and if it's not the case, they will take a decision.

'I always have confidence in myself because it's a big, big mistake to not be 100% involved in what I have to do.

'We have to adjust some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions and more efficiency and I think it will be okay.'

Mac Allister was the scorer as he continued a fine resurgence this season, with Dominik Szoboszlai the supplier after a week where he too had been criticised. The Hungarian whipped a cross towards Mac Allister, which was glanced past Henderson for 1-0.

The former Brighton player ran straight towards the Palace fans behind the goal and taunted the supporters that were once his rivals on the south coast.

Liverpool weathered another storm at the start of the second half and soon found themselves two up. Barcola, who had left lots to be desired in the first half, swapped wings at the break and made his first attack count.

The Frenchman put the after-burners on and motored down the pitch before feeding Wirtz, who composed himself and passed into the net for 2-0. Iraola praised the run of Isak which took him away from the ball but dragged defenders with him to create space for his colleague.

Isak squandered a one-versus-one chance not long after but was not going to miss another one minutes later, when a blisteringly quick counter-attack was started by Trey Nyoni and ended with Wirtz feeding Isak, who skipped past Chris Richards and finished calmly.

The three goals will delight the hierarchy, with all three of the £100m boys – Isak, Barcola and Wirtz – registering at least one goal or assist apiece, one each in Wirtz's case.

Alexander Isak scored the visitors' third in the 89th-minute with this right-footed finish

Eddie Nketiah pulled one back for Palace from the penalty in second-half stoppage time

This victory would not have been possible, though, without Alisson, now 34 and in the final year of his deal. For all the attacking talent at Iraola's disposal, the Basque will be delighted at his team's defensive determination when under the kosh here as Palace had 10 first-half shots.

Iraola knows his team has flaws and they remain a work-in-progress. But despite a few challenging afternoons, they appear to be heading in the right direction.

The same cannot be said for Sage, whose side pulled one back in stoppage time through an Eddie Nketiah penalty after Milos Kerkez committed a careless foul.

Palace were unlucky in this game but the cold, hard truth is that the recent FA Cup and Europa Conference League triumphs feel a world away now as they enter the international break rock bottom of the Premier League.

West Ham also won a European trophy in the last five years and look where they ended up — that should set alarm bells ringing that no success lasts for ever and Palace are not too big for relegation.

Nketiah's goal felt like it was too little, too late and the sage advice for Palace supremo Steve Parish might be a reluctant change in the dugout.

#1153. The hidden treasure in discarded wearable and fast tech

Sales of fast tech like mini fans and disposable e-vapes, as well as wearable health tech such as heart monitors and smartwatches are soaring. They're creating a new e-waste problem but are full of hidden treasure.

From mini fans and the cheap chargers to smartwatches bought as part of a New Year's health kick, some 44% of Europeans own at least six "fast-tech" gadgets. And more than half say they keep unused and broken e-waste items languishing at home or throw them in the regular trash instead of recycling.

That's according to a new report by Brussels-based e-waste association WEEE Forum. It describes fast tech, which is booming, as charging and lighting devices under €10 (circa $11), high-tech items like power banks and fitness trackers, and gadgets and lifestyle appliances like cheap mini blenders and fans, as well as single-use electronic vapes.

"So, these electronics are a bit like fast fashion," Magdalena Charytanowicz, WEEE Forum's Communication Manager, told DW.

Nearly 40% of buyers recalled discarding a fast-tech item without using it at all or within a month of buying it, and nearly 60% said they had used a product for no longer than six months. Yet the vast majority of respondents were generally satisfied with their gadgets despite short-lived functionality.

This suggests consumers accept the "fast-tech bargain" of poor quality that "does the job for a while" and is easily replaced — similar to fast fashion — according to the report.

About 62 million tons of electronics are discarded worldwide annually. "That's the Great Wall of China of e-waste that is produced every year," noted Charytanowicz, adding that the figure is set to grow to 82 million by 2030.

In Europe, roughly 40% of electronic waste is recycled, yet the rate worldwide is just 17%. This means valuable materials are lost, while electronic waste ends up polluting the environment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2022, a million tons of critical raw materials were embedded in the 10.7 million tons of e-waste generated across Europe, including manganese, gold, copper and aluminum.

These materials are at "the center of geopolitical tensions," Charytanowicz said, referring to escalating global tensions over access to rare earths and other critical minerals.

"Even the smallest" devices are worth recycling if they contain a circuit board or battery, she said.

Groups like WEEE Forum say more awareness raising is needed on how to dispose of cheap electronic devices, and that recycling should be made as easy as possible.

But the best way to reduce a product's environmental impact is to extend its lifespan through better design and repair, as recycling raw materials is energy intensive.

Charytonawicz said clearer, harmonized EU rules now under consideration could help improve e-waste collection. The bloc's 20-year-old directive is "not really adapted to the changing reality," she said.

Another growing area of e-waste is digital healthcare. While devices such as diabetes sensors and blood pressure monitors are "transforming healthcare," many are designed to be disposable.

A study published in Nature in December 2025 found sales of wearable healthcare electronics, for example, could reach 2 billion devices annually by 2050, and generate a million tons of e-waste.

Jeremy Faludi, associate professor of sustainable design engineering at TU Delft in the Netherlands, says making health tech — particularly digital devices used in, or issued by hospitals — recyclable or reusable comes with some "much bigger challenges" than normal electronics.

That's in part due to the potential for patient contamination, particularly with digital surgical devices that come into contact with blood or other bodily fluids.

"The way that a lot of things are designed now, you can't recover the stuff because it can't be easily sterilized without the electronics," said Faludi.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He worked on the Digital Health in Circular Economy (DiCE) project, an EU-funded initiative, to help redesign digital healthcare devices to "recover critical materials and reduce environmental impacts without compromising patient safety."

A modular design, for example, allows electronic components to be separated from the parts that need to be replaced between patients, making devices easier to reuse.

The four-year DiCE project, which included citizens, hospitals and manufacturers across nine EU countries, found reusable ECG cables — which connect patients to heart-monitoring equipment — cut environmental impacts by up to 81-94%, for example. The sets are usually designed for single use.

Rules around medical waste can also make reuse and recycling more difficult, particularly when requirements differ between countries and often come down to perceived rather than actual risk, Faludi added. He says some 85% of hospital trash is not infectious but everything ends up in the same bins. Better sorting as well as EU-wide regulations around treating non-infectious hospital waste would help here.

Like with other tech, consumer health devices such as blood pressure and glucose monitors often risk being forgotten in drawers or ending up in the wrong waste, simply because people do not know how to dispose of them, said Charytanowicz of WEEE Forum, which is also involved in DiCE.

Pilot schemes in Belgium, Spain and Slovenia that offered free postal returns and collection machines in public places found that more than 60% of people were willing to return unwanted devices if it was a straightforward process.

"What's really important is the convenience so that it can be integrated in your daily routines," said Charytanowicz, adding that "nudges" such as messages that recycling a device could help the health of another person motivate people to "do the right thing."

James Zou is in the Department of Biomedical Data Science, Stanford University, Stanford, California 94305, USA.

Artificial intelligence has been tremendously useful in science, but, most of the time, it is used for computational work, such as analysing data, making predictions and scouring literature. Carrying out ‘wet laboratory’ experiments — which involve handling liquids, biological material and chemicals — is another matter. An AI system might design a promising biologically active molecule in minutes, but testing it can take weeks or months and requires extensive human effort. In a paper published in Nature, Wu et al.1 introduce AutoDNA, a lab in which AI agents plan and conduct molecular-biology experiments involving DNA, with relatively little human intervention. The work shows how AI systems can begin to close the gap between proposing an experiment and doing it.

#1148. Trump's diesel deal with Russia is unlikely to significantly lower global fuel prices despite expectations of rapid relief

As the world's largest diesel exporter, the US benefits from high prices. At home, however, consumers are feeling the strain of rising living costs. Why Donald Trump's deal with Russia is unlikely to change that.

With or without a deal with Russia, diesel prices on global markets are unlikely to fall significantly anytime soon.

That is the assessment of experts interviewed by DW regarding the latest fuel-supply agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"The main reason for high diesel prices is the war in Iran and the simultaneous disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," said Samina Sultan, a foreign trade expert at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne.

The situation has led to production outages and made fuel shipments "more expensive, less secure and more difficult," she said.

Trump's deal with Russia also has an additional geopolitical dimension, Sultan said: "It causes the wars in Ukraine and Iran to become completely intertwined."

Things are looking up, though. Roughly 13.5 million barrels of crude oil are once again flowing through the Strait of Hormuz a day, according to shipping and commodities analytics firm Kpler.

But for refined products such as diesel, volumes remain far lower at around 677,000 barrels per day, compared with 3.6 million barrels before the war.

Carsten Fritsch, a commodities analyst at Commerzbank, also attributes the price increases to the wars.

"If nothing changes in Ukraine and the Middle East, I see very few ways to resolve these supply bottlenecks," he said.

In a social media post on October 9, Trump announced that he would temporarily suspend some sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel.

He wrote "diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" in a mix of lowercase and all caps.

Russia confirmed the arrangement. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS on October 13 that supplying diesel fuel was "in the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets."

Diesel prices in the US and many EU countries have risen sharply over the past 12 months.

According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), prices in the US have climbed by about 60% and now stand at $6.30 per gallon, equivalent to $1.66 (or €1.49) per liter of diesel.

But even if Russia were able to flood global markets with cheap diesel, prices would not fall nearly as much as they recently rose, something all of the experts contacted by DW agree on.

Many refineries around the Gulf region have suffered disruptions or damage, while transporting fuel via shadow fleets and securing insurance remains costly, cumbersome and risky.

Another key shift is that Russia is no longer the world's largest diesel exporter. In fact, it is facing its own fuel shortages at home.

The US is now the world's biggest diesel exporter. In 2025, it exported an average of 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day, accounting for roughly 15.4% of global diesel exports.

At the same time, Russia fell to second place with a 9.5% share, and that was before major Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries.

Besides the new US-Russia diesel agreement, Trump also recently floated the idea of US diesel export restrictions. But the idea was abandoned because it could lead to even higher diesel prices in the country, according to Samina Sultan.

"There simply is not enough diesel storage capacity in the United States," Sultan said. "Production would have to be reduced, and then prices would rise again."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the US were to impose export restrictions on diesel, buyers in Latin America and the European Union would be hit particularly hard. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, EU countries have increasingly imported diesel from the US instead of Russia because of sanctions.

"An export ban merely redistributes the shortage; it does not solve it," said ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski.

"Global prices would continue to rise, while refineries would scale back production as margins shrink," he added.

Export restrictions aside, few people consider that the US-Russia diesel deal will have any big impact.

According to calculations by the platform The World Data, the promised shipment of 2.2 million barrels of diesel from Russia would not even cover a single day's US diesel demand of roughly 4 million barrels.

Even if all of the diesel volumes announced by Trump were combined, totaling 35.8 million barrels, they would only cover about nine days of US domestic demand.

"I CANNOT OVERSTATE HOW MUCH OF A NOTHING BURGER THIS IS," Canadian oil market analyst Rory Johnston wrote in an all-caps post on X shortly after the announcement.

Russia would normally export almost 10 times that volume if its refinery fleet was not being targeted by Ukrainian drone attacks, he added.

Canada also supplies diesel to the United States. Roughly 80% of all US diesel imports come from its northern neighbor.

Given Trump's verbal attacks on Canada and the ongoing trade dispute, analysts view the prospect of Canada supplying significantly more diesel to the US as highly unlikely.

This piece was originally published in German.

#1144. This is how Enzo Maresca's tactics have left Elliot Anderson exposed with too much to do, writes JACK GAUGHAN... and why £125m Enzo Fernandez must step up and offer much more to solve midfield riddle

Published: 07:00 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 13:08 EDT, 8 November 2026

Manchester City spent £320million on overhauling their midfield over the summer. In doing so, they twice broke their own transfer record. This marked the most aggressive focus on a specific need since the lavish outlay on full backs nine years ago.

All signed weeks before the independent commission’s guilty verdicts were announced, Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernandez and Ayyoub Bouaddi heralded a new era in the City engine room. More energy, vibrancy, dynamism.

Two of them were ready-made replacements for Rodri and Bernardo Silva, with Bouaddi only 18 at the time and purchased as a potential superstar after shooting to global prominence at the World Cup.

But as Enzo Maresca heads into the second international break of the season on the back of three consecutive Premier League defeats, his midfield is the primary area of concern. And has been for a while.

A big fortnight lies in store for City’s manager, whose midfield has been wide open all year. Fine when outscoring opponents – see the 5-3 victory over Sunderland – and it makes for great entertainment yet an obvious gaping chasm when the goals dry up slightly.

The balance has not felt right and Maresca, who has gently batted away persistent questions about the midfield for weeks, must know this.

Elliot Anderson is being asked to do too much and it cost City in the 3-1 defeat at Forest

While studying tapes of all three defeats over the coming days, before City come back after the internationals to host Fulham and then go to Arsenal, he needs to determine a plan moving forward and that will include some tough decisions on individuals and shapes.

Nottingham Forest could have driven a bus through the middle of the park on Saturday night, two goals from counter-attacking situations engineered between the width of the centre circle. Twice the ostensible holding midfielder Anderson tried to nick possession, beaten to it, and City were turned around.

Noises coming from the dressing room suggest that Anderson is effectively being asked to operate as both a No6 and No8 when picked as the deepest of the three, to go and join play high up the pitch. That is Maresca leaning into the England international’s Action Man, everything to everyone style. That also relies on somebody covering for him.

That somebody does not exist in this current setup, Fernandez always too high and wide elsewhere.

So when they lose duels as happened at the City Ground, something the manager openly bemoaned, City are not stable enough to recover.

Liam Delap's fierce finish put Forest 2-0 ahead - and City were left playing catch-up

Club analysts have sat down with Anderson to go over video clips on how best to follow these instructions to the benefit of the team. Watching him, it’s hard not to conclude that this is a quality midfielder being asked to do too much as a single deep midfielder.

England are sweating on the fitness of Marc Guehi as the Manchester City defender battles a hip injury.

Guehi came off at half time of Saturday's 3-1 defeat by Nottingham Forest, with Thomas Tuchel's squad set to link up in London on Monday morning.

With John Stones already out of Nations League ties with Croatia and Spain, Tuchel would be severely light on experience at centre half should Guehi not prove his fitness.

It will produce moments of sheer class – that lung-busting run up the right in Leipzig on Wednesday that bore hallmarks of Kevin De Bruyne, a perfect cross for Erling Haaland’s winner – while also leaving the defence exposed.

An exposed defence lends itself to a heightened chance of individual errors, plenty of those around at the moment, and it was noticeable at Forest that the opening goal came from uncertainty in possession. Josko Gvardiol made the error, eased off the ball by eventual goalscorer Jair Cunha, but the plan cannot be to have the left back with his back to goal and no viable passing options.

When Marc Guehi’s ball went into Gvardiol, Anderson was higher and wider on the right – deep in conversation with Abdukodir Khusanov about how they’d failed to move possession well enough earlier in the sequence – and Rayan Cherki was belatedly trotting back to offer himself.

Fernandez never once enters the frame, even when Cunha is in the box and subsequently wheeling away in celebration. Maresca rejected the suggestion that there is an issue with the team’s build-up on Saturday night.

As Man City look to build from the back in the third minute, Anderson (No 5) is busy delivering instructions to Khusanov (out of shot)...

... it means that when Guehi plays the ball to Gvardiol, he has his back to goal and nobody in midfield to pass to - and is already under pressure

... and with no support, three Forest players swarm and Jair Cunha dispossesses him, leading to him scoring the opening goal

What is clear though is that there is not yet that balance, that this is not yet a unit. Maresca moved to include Bouaddi with Anderson and Fernandez against Brighton – a one-goal defeat – but that acted as detrimental to creativity. If nothing else, Brighton proved that City require either Cherki or Phil Foden on the pitch at all times.

Over the past two games, Fernandez has lurked more menacingly at the back post, offering an additional goal threat rather than just relying on Haaland. That ghosting late run saw him score in Leipzig but for a joint-British record £125million needs to offer so much more. There will be growing calls for Bouaddi’s inclusion as a genuine deep-lying midfielder but it’s unlikely that the teenager can manage the league’s physicality as a single pivot.

The Moroccan has more chance of stamping his authority when alongside somebody else, dovetailing with an Anderson as a two. That leaves Fernandez, whose barnstorming league debut at Old Trafford feels like a long time ago now.

To persist with him, he either dislodges Cherki as the No10 on the promise of far more goals or Maresca drops him back into a more conventional role that allows Anderson to flourish properly.

Something has to give because the unevenness of City’s three is giving the rest of the team uncomfortable jitters.

Greenwood has been Fenerbahce’s best player by far tonight and he tests Alisson. Lukaku finds Greenwood with a pass forward down the left channel and, from inside the Liverpool penalty area, the latter forces Alisson into a decent save.

What started off as an encouraging performance has descended into something ordinary at best for Liverpool. Andoni Iraola says he will not waste any more time thinking about the penalty Liverpool were denied against Arsenal and won’t seek an explanation from Pro Ref. There was a significant fallout following the 1-0 loss at Anfield on Sunday with many judges believing Stuart Attwell, who was VAR, should have consulted match official Andy Madley to highlight an obvious pull by Jurrien Timber that prevented Alexander Isak heading a Bradley Barcola cross.

Liverpool’s head coach explained in the heat of the moment that he would tell his players to go down if they felt contact in the area and Cody Gakpo, the Netherlands international, explained last night in Istanbul it was a message the squad had taken on board.

“As a team, we play pretty fair – maybe we should dive some more like the gaffer said,” Gakpo, who also had claims to be awarded a penalty against Arsenal, explained. “On both occasions you could have given a penalty or a foul, but they decided not. We have to live with the decision. That’s it.”

But as angry as he was with the situation, Iraola has drawn a line on the matter. He is not going to seek out Pro Ref for a discussion – even though he feels a number of decisions have gone against Liverpool this season – and is channelling his energy into other situations.

Iraola said: “I didn’t ask for an explanation and I haven’t received an explanation, no. I told you what you I think about the plays but, honestly, I don’t have the time to [speak to Pro Ref]. I have been preparing for Fenerbahce. It is just two days between games so I have just been focusing on this game and the opposition and how to prepare the team.”

Liverpool have made the long trip to Turkey to take on Fenerbahce on matchday four of the Champions League.

Liverpool enter this fixture having won all three Champions League matches thus far, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal to make it nine points from nine for Andoni Iraola’s side. Liverpool’s five-game unbeaten streak was ended by Arsenal in the league on Sunday. They return to the city where the club enjoyed one of their most memorable nights, beating AC Milan in the Champions League final 21 years ago.

“Istanbul is always going to be very special for Liverpool,” Iraola said. “It is difficult to find a more important night. Tomorrow [tonight] it won’t be easy, you talk about statistics, especially English teams playing here. They have very good players and a very good squad, they know how to play in this competition. We have to start strong in the game. It is very early in the season to establish comparisons. We want to continue how we have done in the Champions League, three games and nine points, it is a good chance to get to 12 points and then finish in the top eight. Champions League away is very difficult.”

In addition to the long-term absentees Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Giovanni, both Ryan Gravenberch and Jeremie Frimpong have missed the trip to Turkey.

Fenerbahce have made a slow start to their Champions League campaign, taking just two points from their opening three fixtures. They have drawn twice against Roma and Slavia Prague at home whilst they suffered a heavy 6-0 loss at Aston Villa. Former Liverpool forward Dirk Kuyt has been appointed their interim coach following the resignation of Ismail Kartal following their recent defeat to arch rivals Galatasaray just over a week ago.

“It is a great opportunity for us to show what we can do,” Kuyt said. “It is also a great opportunity for me, a game between two teams that are very important to me. We have a very good plan, and we have to believe in this plan. No-one who loves Fenerbahce is happy with the current situation, but this is a huge opportunity. We have players who have won the Champions League and the World Cup.”

They come into tonight’s match having lost back-to-back league games since drawing against Slavia Prague on matchday three of the Champions League. They have plenty of former Premier League players in their ranks, including Ederson, N’Golo Kante and Romelu Lukaku.

#1141. Why Chinese tech brands are outpacing Western rivals from EVs to robot vacuums

Do you remember the days when GoPro was synonymous with action cameras?

At its peak in 2015, the US company reigned supreme with around 6.6 million units sold that year and a market share of over 70%. Today, the pioneer is fighting for survival.

GoPro's biggest rivals, DJI and Insta360, entered the action camera market in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Today, they account for more than 90% of global smart handheld camera sales.

Alexander Hannemann, who regularly uses action cameras to film his motorcycle rides, says he switched from GoPro to Insta360 around two years ago.

"The quality is much better than a GoPro, even when I'm speeding up and going into corners at like 80 kilometers per hour," he told DW.

GoPro's case is not an exception. Since around 2010, many Chinese brands have not only caught up but surpassed once-dominant Western rivals across the consumer technology industry, from smart TVs to robot vacuums.

Gone are the days when "Made in China" stood for cheap, mass-produced products.

"China is still making affordable products today," says Chris Pereira, a Canadian entrepreneur and author with over 20 years of experience in China. "But the products are also high quality."

This combination has led to well over half of new consumer tech products globally coming from Chinese suppliers, Pereira adds.

BYD, Xpeng and other Chinese car manufactures sold almost two-thirds of all electric cars last year, surpassing incumbents like Tesla. In robot vacuums, Chinese brands dominate the global market, leaving former pioneer US company iRobot struggling to compete.

So why do Chinese companies increasingly outperform their Western rivals?

Pereira, whose consultancy iMpact helps Chinese companies gain traction overseas, attributes China's success to fierce domestic competition in cities like Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Shanghai; highly integrated supply chains and a can-do business culture that allows companies to innovate; and respond to problems quickly.

Other key reasons for China's competitive edge include unparalleled industrial automation, the strategic use of AI in manufacturing, responsiveness from regulators as well as relatively cheap labor, which together leads to significantly lower production costs and much faster innovation cycles than in the world's most advanced economies.

Joey Cheng, who moved to the US for his PhD studies over 20 years ago, is familiar with both the American consumer and the Chinese producer sides.

While his startup is based in the US, almost all the manufacturing is done in Shenzhen, where a large share of the world's hardware and consumer electronics are made.

"The supply chain in Shenzhen is basically inevitable for cost cutting and quick product development," Cheng says. "Especially as a startup you must get the product out quickly, or you'll get blown out of the water."

Although consumers are flocking to Chinese companies, some reservations persist.

A recent poll found that more than 90% of Europeans do not trust Chinese technology companies with their data, while about 80% distrust US firms. Germans expressed the highest level of mistrust.

Nadine, a German travel blogger who uses DJI and Insta360 products, says she wouldn't use any Asian products at home.

"My home robot vacuum is from a German company for precisely this reason: So the data remains compliant with German regulations. After all, manufacturers can connect directly to the camera," she said, referring to camera and audio hacking incidents involving robot vacuums.

Still, Pereira says that Chinese companies expanding abroad have to pay a "trust premium."

"This trust deficit means that they need to be extra competitive in terms of product and price in order for the market to choose them," he says, adding that the gap can be narrowed by a presence in overseas markets like BYD's first European passenger-car plant, expected to open in Hungary later this year.

Chinese companies say they comply with EU data protection rules. However, domestic security laws in the US and China can require firms to hand over data to authorities, and German officials note limited oversight of whether data is transferred from European servers abroad.

In light of security concerns, trade deficits and China's overall dominance, the US and several other Western countries have hit Chinese imports and companies with tariffs, blacklists and strict requirements. In late July, the Trump administration banned the import of humanoid robots manufactured outside the US.

A representative of Chinese robot maker Primebot told DW that all Chinese consumer tech companies are feeling the effects.

"We might seek cooperation with a local US company. Another potential solution is building a factory there," he said.

European countries and the EU are also weighing more tariffs against Chinese companies.

Chris Pereira foresees that the tariffs will accelerate two trends among Chinese companies: Moving more manufacturing overseas and an increasing focus on challenging top-tier Western brands with premium goods.

"Chinese officials and companies recognize that manufacturing needs to be localized to a certain degree. One reason is to assuage the challenges of exporting, another is to create trust locally," Pereira sums up.

"The other trend is that once duties wipe out the price advantage at the bottom, the margin left is at the top, so Chinese brands are increasingly competing directly with established Western names, where trust matters most."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As China's dominance keeps growing, Western companies are scrambling to find ways to stay competitive.

Kaz Merchant, who works for a UK-based company that imports and exports IT hardware, says smaller companies, in particular, must carve out a geographic niche.

"They need to have their own unique selling point for a certain product, which China might not have for that region. Or they need to partner with a Chinese company," he says.

To Pereira, a key issue Europe needs to solve is regulators' responsiveness.

"Chinese regulators tell you very clearly and quickly what you can do. That speed helps companies iterate and succeed overseas," Pereira says.

"If you're waiting weeks for a response, you're going to lose business."
